speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-28, respecting a certain trade agreement between Canada and Australia.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill now before us, Bill No. S-28, consists of six clauses repealing the Australian Trade Agreement Act, 1931, and containing the usual provisions regarding the making of orders and regulations implementing the agreement, the relationship of the act to other legislation and the coming
4442	HOUSE OF
Australian Trade Agreement Act into force of the act. The new trade agreement is attached as a schedule to the bill.
The decision to review the 1931 trade agreement was made at the commonwealth trade and economic conference in Montreal in September, 1958. The new agreement was negotiated in Canberra in March and April, 1959 by a Canadian delegation led by the late John H. English, deputy minister of trade and commerce. It is the third trade agreement between Canada and Australia, the first having been concluded in 1925 and the second in 1931.
The new agreement does not involve any changes in actual rates of duty from those presently in effect. It does, however, make some important improvements in the type of tariff treatment and the margins of preference which Australia binds or guarantees to Canadian goods. There are also concessions of a similar nature on the Canadian side. In addition, the agreement includes various new provisions dealing with such matters as the application of anti-dumping duties and consultation on economic matters.
The new agreement provides for bindings or guarantees of actual rates of duty on 12 items or subitems in the Australian tariff, whereas no rates of duty were bound under the old agreement. It also provides for guaranteed margins of preference on 53 items or subitems compared with the 33 covered by the 1931 agreement. From the Canadian point of view the new agreement not only provides increased safeguards and improved access for our exports, but establishes a better balance between concessions granted and received.
With respect to Canadian imports from Australia, the effect of the new agreement is to provide for the continuation, without substantial change, of most of the concessions which were accorded to Australia by the 1931 agreement and by a supplementary order in council which became effective October 1, 1937. It also binds in Australia's favour free entry of certain Australian products- notably raw wool, sausage casings and raw sheepskins-which were not covered by the 1931 agreement but which in fact have been free of duty for many years.
The new agreement provides also that Australia shall continue to enjoy the benefits of Canada's British preferential tariff rates in respect of all goods not specifically named. In the case of a number of products of particular interest to Australia the existing margins of preference are bound against reduction. In the case of dairy products, Canada is committed only to accord Australian dairy products the benefits of the British preferential rates of duty or any lower rates accorded to a third country.


In general, the effect of the changes which are proposed in schedule A to the agreement is to bring it up to date and to take account of changes which have taken place during the 29 years since the former agreement was negotiated.
The new agreement modifies the provisions relating to the application by Canada and Australia of anti-dumping duties to one another's goods. In the 1931 agreement each country exempted the goods of the other from their anti-dumping duties. However, in cases where material injury was being done to domestic producers either country could, after three months' notice, apply its general tariff rates. Canada and Australia agree in the new agreement that they will normally not apply anti-dumping duties to one another's products. However, article VI of the agreement provides that in cases of injury to domestic industry there shall be consultations between the two governments, and if a mutually satisfactory solution does not result within 60 days anti-dumping duties may be applied.
There is also a provision in the new agreement establishing procedures under which either government may obtain a release from obligations assumed under the agreement in order to bring about an increase in rates of duty recommended by its tariff board. The article provides for consultation regarding compensation for the concession which is being withdrawn, and if agreement is not reached for the withdrawal of equivalent concessions.
Provision is made for the setting up of consultative procedures to discuss matters arising out of the agreement and also a variety of other questions of importance to the two countries, such as import restrictions and instability in international commodity trade. This should result in much closer co-operation between Canada and Australia in the general field of international trade relations as well as the solution of any specific problems which may arise.
Two committees are being set up in order to implement this part of the agreement, the one in Canberra under the chairmanship of the secretary of the Australian department of trade and the other in Ottawa with the deputy minister of trade and commerce as chairman. To facilitate these arrangements both countries have recently appointed trade officials to one another's capitals.
With regard to consultations concerning import restrictions, hon. members will recall that an exchange of correspondence on this subject between Australian and Canadian authorities was tabled in the house on March 22. These letters set forth certain reciprocal

understandings regarding the use of import restrictions and provide for consultations regarding their application.
When the new agreement is ratified it will run for a period of three years. After this time it may be terminated on written notice of six months by either government. Thus it will provide a stable basis for the development of trade between the two countries during the next three years, and there will then be an opportunity to modify it if this appears necessary in the light of developments over this period.
The conclusion of this new trade agreement comes at a most opportune time from the point of view of Canadian exporters. Earlier this year Australia took a major step toward the removal of the import restrictions which it had been maintaining during the post-war period for balance of payments purposes. Effective February 24 Australia completely eliminated controls from 800 million of its imports, representing about 90 per cent of its total annual imports. Moreover, discrimination against dollar goods was removed from all items except motor vehicles which, it was announced, would be freed from control effective October 1, 1960. Thus in a few months' time Canada will be on exactly the same footing as non-dollar suppliers in the Australian market.
There are about 50 products still under control in Australia from all sources and some of these, such as canned salmon and primary aluminum, are of particular interest to Canada. We are, of course, hopeful that it will be possible for Australia to dismantle these controls altogether before very long.
In recent years Australia's import controls have limited the possibilities for expanding and diversifying our exports to that market and have prevented us from making full use of the tariff preferences which our goods receive there. The liberalization measures which Australia has carried out during the last 18 months in line with decisions reached at the Montreal conference have opened up a new phase in the development of our trade with this sister nation of the commonwealth. Many Canadian goods which have not been seen in Australia for a number of years, such as wrist watches, wallpaper and outboard motors, are again appearing on the market there.
I should like to repeat in this connection some words of Australia's distinguished deputy prime minister and minister of trade, Right Hon. John McEwen, on the occasion of the signing of the new trade agreement. He said:
The increase in the total level of imports into Australia which has resulted from recent steps taken by my government, and the removal of practically all discrimination against the dollar area, should give Canadian exporters an unrivalled
Australian Trade Agreement Act opportunity to expand their sales to Australia. Also this agreement will give opportunities to the greatly expanded industries of Canada to market their manufactured products in Australia. I trust they will take advantage of these opportunities and that forthcoming decades will witness even more significant developments in our mutual trade.
Both our countries are growing vigorously and offer rapidly expanding markets for one another's goods. Businessmen in both countries have been increasingly active in exploring the possibilities for expanding the flow of trade between us. A large Canadian delegation returned a month ago from a two and a half weeks' visit to Australia. In a few days' time we will have the opportunity to extend our hospitality in Ottawa to a 40-man trade delegation, the largest ever to set out from Australia, led by the eminent Australian economist and former high commissioner to Canada, Sir Douglas Copland. This mission has already visited Vancouver, Winnipeg, and Toronto, and is in Montreal this week.
There are already signs that the efforts of Canadian businessmen to expand and diversify trade with Australia are producing results. In the first three months of 1960 our exports to Australia totalled $19 million, compared with $11 million in the same period of the preceding year. In the whole of 1959 our exports to Australia reached $54.2 million, about 3 per cent above the 1958 level, and we sold in the Australian market some 207 individual products compared with 186 in the previous year.
Australia is our second largest market in the commonwealth and the seventh largest world market. It is of special importance as a market for the products of our forests and fisheries, and also for manufactured goods. In recent years our main exports to Australia have been newsprint, wood pulp, lumber, canned fish, motor vehicles, aluminum, asbestos and steel.
Canada is also important as a market for Australian goods. In 1959 our imports from that country totalled $41.2 million, and this figure would be even higher if it included the large quantity of Australian wool which Canada imports through the United Kingdom. Australia's principal sales in the Canadian market are agricultural products such as sugar, dried fruits and wool.
Our two countries have much in common. While we are competitors in some fields, our economies are to a considerable extent complementary. It is therefore logical and mutually advantageous to expand the range and volume of the trade flowing in both directions. In expressing our feelings about Canada's relations with Australia and our hopes for this new trade agreement, I can again do no better than to quote Right

Australian Trade Agreement Act Hon. John McEwen. In a foreword to the attractive brochure issued in connection with the Australian trade commission to Canada he has written:
Canada and Australia are strongly linked through the kinship of the British commonwealth with similar loyalties and similar democratic government. This link also extends to a mutual trading partnership which has stood for a great many years. The recent trade agreement discussions, during which the 1931 Canada-Australia trade agreement was revised, should consolidate even further this close relationship.
I welcome this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to bring before the house the trade agreement with Australia for ratification. I commend it to the attention of hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, in dealing with the bill now before the house to approve the Canada-Australia trade treaty I think there will be a remarkable degree of accord indicated on both sides of the house. As I understand the agreement, it does not introduce any new principle but rather represents the bringing up to date of the trade relations of the two countries, the last agreement having been signed almost 30 years ago.
The agreement itself was quite fully described by the minister, but I attach as much significance to the correspondence exchanged by way of amplification and explanation of the agreement which was tabled in the house some weeks ago. To me the significant provisions are those in the agreement dealing with the matter of consultation and the elaborations of that subject in the correspondence.
After the war the Australian government unfortunately found it necessary to have import controls of one sort or another by reason of their shortage of dollar exchange, and it is timely that this agreement has been signed because, so far as Australia is concerned, there is no longer the same necessity for such controls applying against countries seeking to export to them, which controls I am quite sure they felt were undesirable.
To my way of thinking the machinery of consultation is the important part of this whole relationship, because the necessity of keeping trading relations between the two countries up to date tends to be overlooked in view of the great distance between our two countries; and even though Australia is a very important market for Canada, it is not our most pressing market. I would hope that the minister in discharging his administrative responsibility will do all he can to assure that the machinery of consultation between the two governments is kept in good

Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of this intelligent and industrious octet in this corner of the building to express our support for the principle and purpose of this bill. Like the
Australian Trade Agreement Act previous speaker, I think it is most appropriate that we should be discussing this proposed trade agreement between Canada and Australia at a time when the largest trade mission that has ever visited Canada from Australia, according to press reports, is now visiting Canada under the leadership of Sir Douglas Copland, who everyone knows from his previous service in Canada as high commissioner as a good friend of Canada and one who understands Canadian views and will do his best to promote trade and understanding between the two countries.
I noted, Mr. Speaker, according to press reports that Sir Douglas mentioned that at the present time Canada enjoys a rather big advantage with respect to our trade relationships. Let me say first, with respect to the remarks made by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), who regretted that the duration of the treaty was not for more than three years, that I understand his point of view. However, I think the criticism is rather academic, because if this trade relationship is carried on in the future as it has been in the past there is no question about the arrangement being continued and further treaties signed to the advantage of both countries.
In the opinion of this group this trade treaty will further cement the commonwealth, particularly in view of the fact that Canada will now, on the whole, be placed on an equality with the non-dollar suppliers to Australia. I believe that is quite an advance, Mr. Speaker. This bill also assists in freer trade, which is something in which this group firmly believes. We believe in free trade, as much as possible on a worth-while basis, because we believe that is one of the things that create understanding between countries and work toward peace. According to the minister's statement the purpose is to promote freer trade relations, and the bill is the result of concessions being granted by both sides.
In our opinion the widening of opportunities for consultation is an excellent provision, and also the establishment of these committees, because we live in a world in which there are rapidly changing circumstances. These committees, under the terms of this bill, will now have an opportunity to meet and consult and make the adjustments that are required in the light of changed circumstances and of experience. We think that is all to the good.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that as one coming from British Columbia I may express hope for the further liberalization of trade relationships between Canada and Australia which will provide for increased sales of our lumber and our fish products. As a result of this

Australian Trade Agreement Act new trade treaty I trust we shall have increased sales erf the tree fruits of British Columbia, particularly apples. We have had an expanding market in that direction in recent years. To give credit where it is due, I must say it has been owing to the activity of our trade commissioner in Australia in placing before Australian purchasers and the Australian trade the grades, qualities and quantities of apples that were available from British Columbia, a thorough understanding of our marketing procedures and so on.
In conclusion all I can say is that we are confident that this bill contains the right principle, because it provides for committees representing both governments, for continuing consultation to meet changing conditions and changing circumstances, and for the consequent adjustments. We are certain that the future will indicate that this was a wise step to the advantage of both Canada and our sister nation of the commonwealth, Australia.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to detain the house for any great length of time, but I should not like the discussion of this resolution to be concluded without saying a word in support of it and to repeat what those who have preceded me have said, namely that it is a happy circumstance that it should be introduced and, I hope, given unanimous approval at a time when we are welcoming in Canada an Australian mission headed by one whom we have good cause to know and admire. I refer to the former Australian high commissioner in Canada, Sir Douglas Copland, an extremely stimulating and intelligent person indeed whom we shall be very glad to see in Ottawa again next week.
Australia, of course, is an energetic and developing sister nation in our commonwealth. The minister has already pointed out the growing importance of the trade between our two countries. That trade in the normal course of events should grow as the two countries grow. Its potential is perhaps even more important than its actuality at the present time.
It is interesting to realize in connection with Australian development that the rate of capital investment in Australia over the last two or three years has been even higher than it has been in Canada. I think it has been 27 per cent of the gross national product, whereas in our country I believe the figure is just below that. Perhaps of greater significance is the fact that Australia has not the same kind of at least geographical access to a neighbour which could supply unlimited resources for development if it so desired. So all of this 27 per cent has come


from Australian sources except 10 per cent, whereas in Canada I think only about-and I may be wrong in my figure-70 per cent has come from domestic sources, a fact which I think has an interesting significance in relation to our own situation. As one of the members of the Australian mission is reported as having said the other day, "You have gone too far in your dependence on foreign capital". Perhaps if that capital had been as easily accessible to Australia as it has been to Canada more of it might have gone into that country.
At the same time I think it is also true to say that the Australian government has exercised a kind of control-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-over investment which we have not found so necessary in Canada. In the situation which faces us, with our own greater dependence on foreign capital, it is not likely that we would be able to participate to any great extent, as 1 do not think we have done in the past in this capital development in Australia. Perhaps the time is coming however-and I have seen a reference to this matter recently in connection with the Australian mission- when Canadian subsidiaries of United States corporations could be a source of expansion into Australia rather than have that expansion, when it occurs, come from the parent companies. For one thing a Canadian subsidiary would have more experience in dealing with a smaller market. This is something which in the future may be of some advantage to us.
We talk a great deal, and quite rightly, about the importance to Canada of the development of the freest possible trade in the widest possible Atlantic area-Atlantic free trade; about the building up of the Atlantic economic community. Nothing could be much more important for us than that, of course. But a discussion of this kind makes us conscious of the fact that even the Atlantic area would not be enough, that we have important trading partnerships within the commonwealth. In the step which I hope we are taking to associate Canada with this European development we must not forget that somehow or other we must bring into that association, if it can be done, other nations of the commonwealth so this area will have an even wider expansion than the north Atlantic.
All I need say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, is that we welcome this arrangement. It is perhaps not as far-reaching as it might have been, but it is a useful one. It will help both countries, and I think it will play a good part in strengthening the economic and other relations between the two countries. In that connection perhaps I should reiterate what has already been said on this subject by the

hon. member who just preceded me, namely that we owe a special debt of gratitude to officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of External Affairs who over the years have played such an important role in developing and strengthening these good relationships.

As
a member from British Columbia, and more specifically from the constituency of Vancouver South, may I say that we are particularly interested in this trade agreement. I was greatly struck by the words of the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke about our preoccupation with Atlantic matters and pointed out that on the other side of this nation lies an equally vast ocean with equally great trade opportunities awaiting development.
This is a new agreement which will bring a measure of stability, so that importers and exporters will know the conditions under which they can conduct business. There is the relaxation of currency controls, and the fact that over the last few years we have improved communications with Australia to a tremendous extent. We now have modern, fast ocean-going liners complete with refrigeration space making regular sailings between Vancouver and Australian and New Zealand ports. The Canadian flag air carrier is based in Vancouver, with services by air to New Zealand and Australia.
We on the west coast are tremendously interested in the development of increased trade with Australia and other countries in the Far East. We welcome the thought left with us by the minister, namely that even the few remaining items which affect us to a considerable extent will shortly be released from currency restrictions.
We realize that trade is a two-way street. We realize that if we are going to sell, we must buy. The economy of Australia is largely complementary to ours. We welcome the thought of increased trade both coming in and going out.
We think this is a step toward that larger pattern of trade, particularly within the commonwealth, which is getting away from a purely North American trade pattern. We welcome this agreement and we are sure that in years to come this trade will increase and not only will double but may triple and go even further than that.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a few words in welcoming and supporting second reading of this bill, respecting a certain trade agreement between Canada and Australia. I do so from two bases, one sentimental and one materialistic.
2,	1960
Australian Trade Agreement Act
The sentimental basis is because I have been told by some that I am half kangaroo. I think I am one of the blessed men in that my mother was born in Australia, my father was born in England, and I live in Canada. If you can beat that combination I would like to know how. So I say that on a sentimental basis I am very happy about the bill now before us.
I appreciate very much the opportunity I had last fall of spending some six weeks in Australia as a member of the commonwealth parliamentary association. In that period of six weeks I had the opportunity of talking with some of the premiers and cabinet ministers of the various states of Australia, and I became quite disturbed at some of their indications as to a change in trade relationships between Canada and Australia, particularly because I felt it would have an effect on my province of British Columbia. It is because of what I heard there that I want to express my personal appreciation of the visit to Canada of the Australian trade delegation, and I was pleased to read in the press their enthusiasm about what they maintain is the success of their mission. I too look forward to meeting with some of them this coming week.
I would like to suggest through you, Mr. Speaker, that trade is not a one-way street. Trade is something which has to be worked for and fought for, and in expressing our terrific appreciation at the visit of the Australian trade commission I think in turn we should send one just >as strong, virile and enthusiastic to Australia, and not only to Australia but to other parts of the commonwealth as well.
Very briefly I want to support what the Leader of the Opposition mentioned, namely that Canada is an exporting nation. Canada depends upon exports for its very livelihood and standard of living. We have already seen the development in Europe of the Inner Six and the Outer Seven; and if we read the journals of the world we can see the possibility -the probability-of other economic formations being brought into being, perhaps in the Latin American countries as well.
This poses a very serious problem to Canada. We must give consideration to these developments, but I believe that something we can do now is to have a closer relationship and greater exchange between governments and industry, between members of the commonwealth, because there in the commonwealth I think lies the greatest economic expansion in the world in the way of transfer from one country to another of the produce which we are able to export.

Australian Trade Agreement Act
I would just like to say that sentimentally I welcome this agreement. On a material basis I welcome it, though I certainly hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will see to it that we do not remain satisfied just with the passage of a trade agreement which will be in effect for three years but that we will reciprocate with Australia and send a trade mission ourselves into every part of the commonwealth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will just take a few minutes to conclude this debate which has shown that the house is unanimous in recording its approval, as it will in a few minutes, of the Canada-Australia trade agreement. We have had an expression of opinion here today which I think indicates the bond that links Canada and Australia very closely, not only the bond of commonwealth attachment but the bond which is established through trading relations which have been good over the years.
I think the trade mission which is arriving on Sunday and will be in Ottawa on Monday will appreciate the fact that the House of Commons has acted in this manner today. The measure before us is of importance, but by the good sense of the house we are not spending overly much time on it. That is not because we do not realize that this matter affects greatly the economies of both Australia and Canada; I think it is because we believe that the job has already been done by those who discussed the trade agreement in the conferences which were held, and it is left now to the House of Commons to put its stamp of approval on a first class piece of work which was done by the officials on both sides. Our trade with Australia is important and we hope it will grow, just as they hope their trade with us will expand.
I mentioned in the course of my earlier remarks that a large group of Canadian businessmen have been in Australia on a trade mission of their own and have just returned. I hope before too long it will be possible for us to send to Australia another trade mission in order to further explore the possibilities of trade with that country; and in the light of the present agreement, with air travel now available, it is possible to expand our trade activities around the world as has been suggested. Later on this session I hope to be able to put before the house some ideas we have in that regard.
The hon. member for Ottawa West asked for an explanation of the appointment of


officials in the two capitals. We have had trade commissioners in Australia stationed in Sydney and Melbourne, I think it is, but it seemed advisable to put a third man in the capital city, and Mr. Nickson of our department recently arrived in Australia. Similarly the Australian government has placed a commercial counsellor here in Ottawa. The advantage of that arrangement is this, and we do it in other countries of the world. The commercial counsellor living in the capital city can readily get in touch with departmental officials on matters which are of concern. We had in mind here that the problem of consultation would be met immediately by having on the spot in the capital city of each country a commercial representative. Both this country and Australia have quickly taken up that idea and those appointments have been made.

Just before the minister leaves that point, I wonder if I might ask him a question; I want to clear up the matter. As I understand it these new trade officials are in addition to the existing trade officials in each country; it is not just a change of organization?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member is quite right; they are in addition to the trade commissioners already active in the two countries.
Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, the question arose as to the length of the agreement. It is stipulated in one of the terms that it runs for three years. The 1931 agreement had a provision which stated that it would run for one year and thereafter until notice was given, and it ran for 29 years. This trade agreement, which contains a stipulation that it will run for three years, with similar notice before it is terminated, may have a very long life ahead of it. I hope it has.
I believe this marks a further step forward in our trade relations with one of our good trading customers. I can assure the Australians-and I will tell the mission this when it arrives on Monday-that Canadian businessmen will be just as keen as they are to expand business between the two countries. We have things they need, and they have materials and foodstuffs that we can use in Canada. There is a chance for businessmen in the two countries to get acquainted through trade mission activities. Behind those trade missions is the approval of both governments, as is evident from this trade agreement which is a substantial improvement over the earlier agreement. The way is clear to the advance ment of trade between Canada and Australia

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, reference to the blue book on estimates will show that the main estimates for 1960-61 of the Department of Transport and the several other agencies reporting through me amount to $250,912,244. The total figure last year was $269,136,950. The greater part of the indicated decrease of approximately $19 million pertains to the department proper, and in the course of my remarks I shall draw attention to the major items included in the decrease.
During the past few years I have dealt with these estimates according to the three main services of the department, namely canals, marine and air. This format was selected because it made for ease of reference to the blue book. From the tenor of the remarks made by hon. members in the past I gathered that they found the format satisfactory.
Before turning to the canals service, however, let me deal with the matter of the size of our departmental establishment. Last year I reported a total strength of 13,407 employees for all positions, either full time or part time. This figure was increased to 13,620 in last year's supplementary estimates. The various programs covered by the estimates now before this committee will require the employment of 14,196 individuals, or an increase of approximately 4 per cent. In brief, the increase is related to what may be referred to as normal growth arising from the operation of additional ships, airports, navigational aids, etc.
Turning now to the canals service, it will be noted that the four votes appearing on page 73 total slightly under $5 million. This means we contemplate a reduction in expenditure of close to $2,500,000 as compared to the figure for last year. This substantial change is related partly to some expected improvement in operating costs of the nontoll canals transferred to the St. Lawrence seaway authority. Mainly, however, it is due
Supply-Transport
to the completion of a number of large construction projects on those canals for which moneys were voted last year. An example of this was the bridge across the Lachine canal at Ville St. Pierre; $350,000 was voted for that work. The closing of the Soulanges canal is another significant contributing factor.
There are two capital items which stand out in these canal appropriations. First, we are providing $270,000 for the government's contribution toward the new high-level bridge at Kars, which will replace our old swing bridge and fixed bridge spans on the Rideau canal. Second, a further $530,000 is included for rehabilitating the old bed of the second Welland canal. This is a project we have embarked upon following entry into agreement with the several municipalities concerned.
Total funds needed for our marine operations will approximate $43 million. The appropriation for administration, operation and maintenance of our departmental fleet, as well as the chartering of vessels to supplement that equipment, accounts for more than 40 per cent of the figure I have just mentioned.
This administrative responsibility extends to the design, construction, operation, repair, maintenance, etc., of vessels engaged in many different types of work. These operational roles include supply of lighthouses on coastal and inland waters, operation of a weather station in the Pacific ocean, icebreaking and ice patrols, sea transportation of supplies to the D.E.W. line, the mid-Canada line, joint weather stations, and stevedoring at northern points of call.
As would be expected in a vote of this size and general scope in which there are 17 different kinds of expenditures, we find various increases and decreases. The net change, though, is quite small, comparatively speaking; $490,654, to be exact. On the increase side, the chief change pertains to salaries and wages, which are up some $768,000, and this is due to a 10 per cent salary revision for ships' crews approved in 1959, and the commissioning this year of the new icebreaker John A. Macdonald. This diesel-electric, triple screw icebreaker, powered by engines developing 18,000 horsepower, will stand comparison with any icebreaking ship in the world. As for the decreases, these relate mainly to a sharply decreased volume of cargo to be transported to Frobisher and some D.E.W. line stations because of completion of large construction projects. During the 1959 shipping season the total sealift to the many northern points, that is to say for all government departments and for United States government account, amounted to no less than 102,000 tons.

Supply-Transport
Before leaving this particular vote I wish to mention one development of the past year which I am sure will meet with your approval. When I explained our main estimates last year I referred to our take-over in 1959 of the sealift to D.E.W. line stations on the east coast of Baffin island. I stated this meant that Canada would then be performing the entire sealift for D.E.W. line stations on Canadian soil. This program of progressive take-over will be extended even further in 1960. In recent months an agreement has been reached between the Department of Transport and the United States air force whereby we have undertaken to provide transportation of the supplies and equipment for the several Gap-Pine stations along the Labrador coast. It is certainly gratifying to note the increasing capability being demonstrated by Canadian personnel, both commercial and governmental, in the performance of this difficult work. I would like to take this opportunity of commending, for their splendid cooperation, the United States government agencies with which we have been working. Unquestionably that spirit of co-operation has greatly facilitated the task of my department.
During the past year our program for the construction of new vessels and repair of existing vessels has gone forward quite rapidly. Consequently we are planning in terms of a substantial reduction in capital outlay. Since our 1959-60 estimates were approved we have accepted deliveries of several ships. The larger of these, apart from the Sir John A. Macdonald, are the Camsell, which will be the first Canadian icebreaker assigned to support shipping in the western Arctic; two shallow draft, icebreaking and buoy vessels with search and rescue qualities, namely the Simon Fraser, operating from Victoria, and the Tapper operating from Charlottetown; three units, the Sir William A lexander working out of Halifax and the Sir Humphrey Gilbert and Wolfe working out of St. John's, Newfoundland, on supply work and light icebreaking; and the Alexander Henry, a supply light icebreaker ship for service in the upper great lakes, based at Parry Sound.
Residents of the immediate areas will no doubt be pleased to learn that the two ferry vessels, one for the Pelee Island-Ontario service and the other for the Bell Island-Newfoundland service, will be delivered in the very near future. Our proposed program contemplates preparation of plans and specifications this year for certain additional units, particularly replacements for two or three more of our older agency supply ships and possibly replacements for our ocean weather station ships. Among the items
[Mr. Hees.J
presently under study is a cable-laying ship would would be strengthened for icebreaking work as well.
Regardless of my expressed intention to follow the order in which the various departmental services are listed in the blue book, I wish to mention at this point an item actually covered by vote 425. This vote is somewhat similar in that it pertains to ship construction, in this case auto-ferry vessels. In December, 1959 a contract for very close to $3 million was awarded to Halifax Shipyards. It was for the construction of a ferry with capacity for 68 automobiles and 300 passengers which will ply between Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. The three ferries now in use include two which were built some 40 years ago. For this reason and, furthermore, because of the continued growth in traffic, construction of this additional ship is considered essential. We are seeking approval of payments totalling $1,860,000 to be made in this fiscal year.
Operation and maintenance of aids to navigation is a work which continues from year to year at an unusually consistent rate. This will be the case again during the coming year. The estimated outlay of $6 million provides for a program basically the same, both as to volume and make-up.
During the past few years we have been pushing ahead with a program of replacing the wharves and buildings located at our marine agency depots. This work of rehabilitation is essential because the existing structures are very old and quite inadequate to meet present day requirements. This program may take up to 10 years to complete, but it is aimed at providing at such ports as St. John's, Newfoundland; Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island; Dartmouth, Nova Scotia; Saint John, New Brunswick; Quebec, province of Quebec; Sorel, Quebec; Prescott, Ontario; Parry Sound, Ontario; Victoria, British Columbia; and Prince Rupert, British Columbia, a complex consisting of a modern wharf, office and stores building, shops building, etc.
Up to the present time very satisfactory progress has been achieved. This type of construction must be phased over a period of approximately three years in each instance. The stages of construction on some of these projects are such that there will be a reduction in expenditure in 1960-61. For example, the sum of $400,000 was required last year for the new wharf at the St. John's, Newfoundland agency. The second stage of that project is the construction of the office and stores building, and approximately $80,000 will be sufficient for this purpose.

The granting of wage increases in 1959 to ships' personnel is a consideration which also had to be covered in appropriations related to deficits on ferry services. Examination of those items will disclose that we are providing approximately $800,000 additional for the Borden-Tormentine and Sydney-Newfound-land ports ferry operations, and the wage increase accounts for most of that revision. Whilst referring to ferry operations I might mention a rather sizeable expenditure of $400,000 to improve conditions at North Sydney, where heavy congestion of shipments occurred due to inadequacy of railway trackage. To remedy this it is proposed to lay additional trackage and lengthen five existing yard tracks.
Improvement of facilities and equipment required to expedite and facilitate traffic moving to Newfoundland coastal points is being attended to as rapidly as possible. I spoke last summer of our intention to proceed with construction of two passenger-cargo vessels. One of these will be ready in the fall of 1960, the other in the spring of 1961. Whereas $800,000 was allotted for the wharves and freight sheds at Corner Brook and Lewisporte, we must provide well over $2 million to cover the next stage of the work.
I shall now attempt to cite the highlights of our air services, the listing for which begins on page 77. I use the word "attempt" intentionally because this particular service embraces a wide and varied assortment of responsibilities and operations. It is a role which has grown tremendously in size and nature as transportation by air continues its explosive expansion.
The aggregate of the several appropriations related to our telecommunications branch is down slightly from last year, the reduction being just under 4 per cent. The major part of this change is related to the construction or acquisition of buildings and equipment for radio aids to air and marine navigation. Nevertheless the proposed capital outlay is very substantial, for it totals $12,252,000. Something like $2 million of this will be devoted to extension of our program for the installation of instrument landing systems to facilitate the landing of aircraft under poor weather conditions. We are estimating $1.9 million for new or improved low and high frequency aids such as marine radio beacons and non-directional beacons for the various airways across Canada.
In the make-up of this vote the term "communications" appears frequently, and some $5.5 million is allotted for this. The types of equipment are far too numerous for me to attempt any general enumeration. One of the
Supply-Transport
very large requirements is for the installation of transmitters at marine stations where the existing equipment, in many cases as old as 40 years, does not meet the frequency tolerances demanded. Also, at many aeradio stations in northern Canada the present high frequency equipment is subject to blackouts caused by sun spot activity. To assure reliable communications we must supplement with low frequency equipment. The construction of dwellings for personnel at isolated or semi-isolated locations will cost upward of $1.5 million.
The estimated combined costs of both administering and operating our meteorological service in 1960-61, as well as attending to the necessary capital requirements of that service, differ very little from last year's costs. It is true that the printed estimates show a very substantial increase, an increase of $2,325,000 to be exact. However, the actual increase is far less. This year we have included approximately $2 million for services we provide on behalf of the Department of National Defence. In previous years this amount was incorporated in national defence estimates.
Before leaving the meteorological estimates, I do wish to refer to a subject of which I have made mention on numerous occasions. Recruitment of properly qualified personnel for the meteorological service has for the past several years been indeed one of our most difficult problems. Individuals possessing the required qualifications are in demand in other quarters such as in the teaching profession. Recently we have granted salary increases which we expect will improve matters. Further improvement in this connection is under way, and we are carrying out a long term program with respect to recruitment and training. We are very hopeful that these measures will tend to overcome our difficulties, but it appears as though it will take a few years to remedy the situation.
During the course of the statement I gave to the committee last year I pointed out that we were seeking approval of funds for civil aviation requirements which were 17 per cent in excess of those voted for the previous year. For the coming year, I am happy to report, we have managed to plan a program which dollar-wise represents a reduction of between 8 per cent and 9 per cent. It is a program designed to satisfy what we believe to be the most urgent demands of aviation. It will not, mind you, begin to satisfy all quarters. One has to be in close touch daily with the situation to form any true appreciation of the number, variety, extent, etc. of the demands presented by this, the jet age. Many of the problems are obvious to every

Supply-Transport
one of us-longer, wider and stronger runways, bigger aircraft, larger air terminal buildings, more convenient parking areas, and so forth. This is not so, however, with what one might call the hidden requirements.
Air traffic control is a good case in point. Ten years ago controlled landings and takeoffs were occurring in Canada at the rate of 800,000 per year but in the coming year the number will exceed 3| million. Add to this the factor of jet aircraft travelling at three times the speed. The old system involving elaborate display boards in control centres with slips of paper indicating position, altitude and speed of aircraft is being superseded by technological developments utilizing various types of radar, the transfer of radar pictures to closed circuit television, and possibly the adoption of electronic computers to perform speedily the wide variety of calculations.
Here is another clear-cut illustration of the demands generated by technological advancement in aircraft design. Very recently we have taken steps to establish a new high altitude airway, above the 24,000 foot level, for the use of jet aircraft exclusively. Air traffic control is but one of the demands; yet the expenditure this year will total over $7 million, including services and facilities supplied to the Department of National Defence but paid for by the Department of Transport.
Another example I might cite is that of aircraft rescue and fire fighting services. Here we have a problem to which intensive study has been and is being given by all countries directly affected by the advent of jet aircraft. Obviously this task is magnified by the weight, passenger capacity and landing speed of the jet airliner, even though at many airports the R.C.A.F. performs a major part of the function. To illustrate the expansion in this area, we have ordered 13 additional large fire fighting trucks to supplement the existing 78. At present we employ 137 fire fighters at airports but now we must hire an additional 102 and the wage bill alone will reach approximately $1.5 million yearly. Over and above this we have on order a number of crash trucks, water tenders and aerial ladders.
In the area of construction associated with new or improved air terminal buildings, runways, landing strips, heating plants, entrance roads and the many other facilities that go into the make-up of the modern airport, we are forging ahead very satisfactorily. During the coming year the terminal buildings at Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa and Regina will be ready for operation and we will be proceeding with the initial stages of the new layout of the airports at Winnipeg and Edmonton.

Despite the unceasing demand for the many improved facilities, we have managed, in keeping with the general budgeting policy, to prepare a 1960-61 program entailing an expenditure of approximately $8 million less than the appropriation approved for 1959-60. The proposed outlay totals $52 million, of which $18 million is earmarked for airport terminal buildings. If time permitted I would single out for the committee's information some of the more outstanding projects interspersed among the list, which runs to several pages. In lieu of that I have had prepared a statement enumerating the projects in the $100,000 or over category for which provision is made in this vote but which are not shown in the details given in the blue book. I shall be glad to furnish a copy of this to any member desiring it. I might also add that the summary details our marine construction projects as well.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the committee will be grateful to the minister for the excellent statement he has just given to us which will assist us very materially in the discussion of these estimates. I think the committee will also be happy to have before it a list of the projects costing over $100,000 which the department intends to put into being during the course of the present fiscal year.
The minister, as has been the case in the past, has divided his statement, generally speaking, under three heads, namely water, air and rail facilities. As one listened to the remarks made by the minister one matter primarily attracted our attention and that is the tremendous amounts that are being spent from year to year by the Department of Transport. While it is true that there has been a decrease this year, mainly, I think, because of the large expenditure last year for the St. Lawrence seaway, the expenditures which are made by this huge department are indicative of the importance of the part it is playing in the field of transportation.
There is no doubt in the minds of those of us who sit on this side of the house, and I think this applies to most hon. members who have given the subject of transportation any thought, that because of the age in which we live the department must of necessity take on greater importance, and I am wondering whether the government has given consideration to a division of the responsibilities of the department. I say this with all deference to the minister. It is not that I think that he is incapable of fulfilling the duties which a minister of transport must fulfil, but I think that consideration should be given to this matter having regard to the very important duties and responsibilities that fall on the

Department of Transport. This may not be a popular suggestion so far as some members of the department are concerned but nevertheless I think that if the government has not already given this matter consideration it should do so because of the tremendous importance of the department and because of the fact that it is gathering greater and greater momentum as time and technological development go on.
It may well be that the department could be divided into two parts with railway and canal services forming one department and aviation forming another. The minister will say that this is not a novel or new idea. In fact it is not because I know that before we left office in 1957 serious consideration was being given by the former prime minister to a division of the department although not necessarily along these lines. It seems to me that the duties and responsibilities of the department are such that as time goes on the importance of the department, if not in this year then certainly in the near future, will almost compel the government to divide these responsibilities into at least two parts.
I come to another matter with which the minister did not deal, unfortunately. I would have thought that in the course of his statement the minister would have given some indication of the policies of the government with reference to certain aspects of his department. What is the policy of the government with reference to air services? What is the policy of the government with reference to bilateral air agreements? What is the policy of the government in the field of scheduled and non-scheduled air services? There has been not the slightest indication by the minister on this occasion, and I am sorry to say on previous occasions, of these policies, and because of certain matters to which I have referred in the past and to which I intend to refer briefly now, there should I think be a clear-cut declaration of policy on the part of the government in so far as these fields are concerned.
I think that had the policy been defined by the minister it would have been much easier for those of us who sit on this side of the house, and who like to be constructive in our criticism, to have disposed more quickly of the matters that are under discussion at the moment. On prior occasions I stated that the government was giving away Canadian sovereignty in the air, and that it was discriminating against small air lines in favour of the larger, more powerful ones and, in turn, because of that, the government was discriminating against the outlying regions of our country. At that time the minister
Supply-Transport
made light of my remarks and passed them over as being nonsensical or ridiculous.
I am sorry that he felt disposed to deal with them in that manner because the events that have taken place since have indicated that the remarks made at that time were not only serious but have been supported by the evidence which was given in a committee of the house. I think it was stated by the minister on one occasion that I spoke on behalf of monopoly and vested interests. Unfortunately for the air lines concerned, it now turns out that it is the converse which is true. Not only have the smaller air lines become apprehensive of what is taking place in the field of aviation, but Trans-Canada Air Lines particularly have become extremely anxious about the position in which they find themselves because of the policy of the government with reference to bilateral air agreements, consequent upon the policy of the government in the field of international aviation.
I should like to refer for a moment now to the evidence given before the committee on railways, air lines and shipping by the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines. I made the statement in the house at one juncture that because of the budget for Trans-Canada Air Lines, which the minister tabled in the early part of the session and which indicated that in order to purchase new equipment the amount of many available would be the sum of nil dollars from net income; I had not drawn a conclusion at the time, but I asked a qusetion as to whether or not this might well be indicative of a position in which Trans-Canada Air Lines might find itself because of the international aviation policy of the government. The minister thought that that conclusion was not justified. None the less when Trans-Canada Air Lines tabled its report for 1959 it indicated that its net income was the lowest for all time in its history, namely about $152,000.
Later when the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines gave evidence before the committee he indicated that the loss of revenue from the operation of B.O.A.C. into Toronto would amount to $6 million gross revenue per year, and that the loss of revenue arising out of the recent bilateral route which was awarded by the government and the onward rights which were awarded to Air France and Lufthansa from Montreal to Chicago would amount to an actual loss to Trans-Canada Air Lines of $200,000 per year. The statement which was made at the time, and which I repeat now, is that because of these bilaterals which granted Lufthansa, Alitalia and Air France onward rights from Montreal

Sup p ly-Transport
to Chicago which T.C.A. does not possess, and who are going to compete directly with T.C.A., there would eventually be a substantial loss. In this particular case Trans-Canada Air Lines has not got a non-stop flight from Montreal to Chicago. It must come down at Toronto and is, therefore, at a loss in so far as competition goes with these foreign air lines and because of the policy of the government in this field Trans-Canada Air Lines has been detrimentally affected.
While I am not able to go as far, perhaps, as some of the witnesses went before the committee on railways and shipping, I believe it is safe to conclude that in the year 1960 the financial position, the profit and loss position of Trans-Canada Air Lines will be worse than it was in 1959. I should like to place on the record here, for the benefit of those who were not members of this committee, the questions and answers which can be found on page 340 of proceedings No. 3 of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, for Thursday, March 31, 1960:

The anxieties which were expressed at the time by those of us who took part in this debate have now been confirmed by the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines. So much so have they been confirmed that the president has

found it necessary to enter into a pooling arrangement with B.O.A.C. in connection with the north Atlantic services performed by T.C.A. The loss to T.C.A. from the granting of these onward rights is substantial. I think that consideration ought to be given at once by the minister to a renegotiation of these bilateral agreements or, in the alternative, to a renegotiation of the bilateral agreement with the United States which would give the T.C.A. and other Canadian carriers the right to operate into certain lucrative airports of the United States and would offset the losses that have been caused by the negotiation of these recent bilateral agreements.
It seems to me that all of this has been done in the name of competition. No one was more anxious that there should be competition than was my friend the Minister of Transport when he sat on this side of the house. However, when he moved over to the other side of the house he had an expert look into this whole field of transportation and there was produced the Wheatcroft report. I have no fault to find with the Wheatcroft report. On the contrary; I think the Wheatcroft report is excellent in many respects. Unfortunately, however, the minister has not seen fit to follow that report. The competition to which Trans-Canada Air Lines is being subjected is going to mean financial loss to the company.
But I believe this position of competition also applies in the field of domestic air services. I think it is unfortunate that the minister did not see fit to indicate to the committee what the government policy was with reference to those services. I think it can also be said that in this field of domestic air services there is on the part of the government, through the initiation of the minister, a tendency to allow far too much competition. That tendency was indicated by the decontrol of groups C and B, the one on July 18, 1958 and the other on December 21, 1958. The opening up of these two categories of air services to competition was a serious matter. The result has been a tremendous number of bankruptcies. Certainly there have been a larger number of bankruptcies than anyone would have expected would occur.
I placed on the order paper a starred question in connection with this matter. The answer the minister gave was that six aviation companies had gone into bankruptcy since July 18, 1958, the date of the announcement of the decontrol of group C; that 38 air companies had applied for suspension of services; that 15 companies had applied for cancellation of their permits; and that 15 companies had had their permits cancelled. It seems to me that this is cleanly indicative

of this new policy of competition in every field which has meant that many of these companies have been unable to carry on. They had difficulties previously but those difficulties became insurmountable and it was not possible for them to carry on; hence these bankruptcies and these suspensions of services.
This is exactly what the air industries and transport association foreshadowed in their brief to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport at the annual association meeting which they held in Montreal in October of last year and again in a subsequent meeting which they held in Victoria some short time ago.
There is also an extremely unsatisfactory situation with regard to Autair Helicopter Services. Surely the minister has not given the house a satisfactory answer in so far as this company is concerned. I have no intention of repeating what I said on an earlier occasion dealing with the subject of Autair Helicopter Services. However, I want to say one thing, namely that there is in existence an air transport board which functions in accordance with the terms of the Aeronautics Act. I am sorry to tell the minister that he has not allowed the air transport board to function in accordance with the terms of this act but has interfered with the functions of the air transport board on at least two occasions. The first occasion is that of Autair Helicopter Services and the other is that of Georgian Bay Airways Limited.
In the case of Autair Helicopter Services, an application was made by that company before the air transport board. A public hearing was held by the board in Montreal and after careful consideration by the members of the air transport board they declined to grant the application. However, upon appeal the minister overruled the board. I say now, as I said before, that the minister should not have interfered in a judicial matter. Had it been purely a question of fact, that would have been an entirely different matter. However, it was not purely a question of fact; it was a matter of a judicial nature. When the Aeronautics Act was passed by this parliament I think the intention clearly was that while an appeal lay to the minister in certain circumstances, in so far as the legal aspect was concerned the matter was for the air transport board to determine.
The result has been extremely unfortunate in so far as this company is concerned and in so far as the air transport board is concerned. With the overruling of the board by the minister we have no proof of financial responsibility. A number of accidents have taken place. I believe there have been seven, four in 1959 and three already in 1960, in connection with Autair Services Limited.
Supply-Transport
A letter written by the air transport board to Autair Helicopter Services has gone unanswered. No attention has been paid to this regulating and governing body by an air services corporation which exists and which is subject to the jurisdiction of the board.
I would like to put this letter on Hansard. It is dated February 4, 1959 and was obtained in answer to a notice of motion tabled in this house. It is addressed by the secretary of the air transport board to Autair Helicopter Services and reads:
Dear Sir,
This is further to our letter of January 7th in connection with the removal of the restriction limiting your company to the use of certain helicopters under board decision No. 1111.
Our audit section finds that it cannot make a proper study of your application because it ha* no up to date financial information other than operating reports for the period from commencement of operations to December 31, 1958. The following information should be provided:
(1)	A balance sheet of Autair Helicopter Services Ltd. as at December 31, 1958.
(2)	A consolidated balance sheet of Autair Helicopter Services Ltd. and subsidiaries as at December 31, 1958.
(3)	Full information regarding all helicopters acquired or to be acquired since the date of the above balance sheet, including type or types, estimated cost and proposed method of financing purchase.
(4)	Full information regarding terms of repayment of any long term debts which may be included in the above suggested balance sheets.
As soon as the above has been received, your application will be further processed.
As far as I know there has not only been no reply to that letter, but there has been an utter and total disregard by an aircraft company operating in this country under the jurisdiction of the air transport board of that governing body. If I am wrong in that assumption I hope the minister will correct me, but I gathered from the information which was obtained earlier that Autair Helicopter Services paid no attention whatsoever and carried on as if the air transport board had never existed at all. In fact, not only did they carry on; they had been operating in the province of Quebec without a licence for a period of several months. I made that statement on an earlier occasion and I repeat it now. The minister said that they did not operate with his knowledge and that may well be; but the point is that the air transport board has in its possession information which would indicate that they did operate without a licence and that the owner of that corporation operated with a private licence only. That certainly is contrary to the rules and regulations established under the Aeronautics Act and applicable to other aircraft companies in Canada.

Supply-Transport
I think the minister should not have interfered with the decision of the board, because if he had not interfered with the decision of the board this company would have either had to abide by the regulations of the air transport board and its procedures or it would not have been able to operate at all.
There is a great deal more than that in connection with this matter. This company has had its insurance cancelled twice. It has also obtained from the government, through the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, a very important contract on the polar shelf involving several hundred thousand dollars. What about these professional men, these workers skilled and otherwise, who are being transported by this company in the north, that not only has had its insurance cancelled but which presently is insured by an unrecognized company in the United States? From the information I have indications are that this company may also cancel the insurance of the company as they have been unable to find any insurance adjuster to handle the accidents which were listed by the minister which took place in 1960.

speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent to the hon. member continuing?
