speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Thank you. I was under the impression that I had unlimited time; I am apparently in error. I am grateful to the committee and I will try and shorten this as much as I can.
I was going on to say that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys gave indication some time ago that this company had had experience on the D.E.W. line. His statement was that the pilots of Autair Helicopter Services had had experience on the D.E.W. line. The information I have is that at the time the contract was awarded and this company was preparing to leave for the polar shelf, which was in April, 1960, there were three pilots in the employ of that company. One of them had a total experience of bush flying of 30 days which he had acquired at Knob Lake three years ago; neither of the other two pilots on the polar continental shelf contract had had any previous Arctic experience.
I think the least the minister can do is to hold an investigation, as he was asked to do by those of us who sit on this side of the house. He should hold an investigation

at least for the safety of those people who may be transported on the helicopters of this company. Surely this is not asking too much. If we were asking this with no evidence of what had transpired I think the minister would be well within his rights in refusing. But we are asking an investigation of a company that has had no experience in operating on the polar shelf; that has already had seven accidents; that has had its insurance cancelled twice; and, most important of all, it is a company whose application was turned down by the governing body in the Department of Transport dealing with these applications after a hearing held in Montreal. For that reason I again say that the minister was in error in overruling the air transport board, in granting the application, and that because of the reasons I have given, which I believe to be serious, there should be a full investigation by the minister into the operations of this company.
Before I resume my seat I would like to say a word about Georgian Bay Airways Limited. This to my mind is a more serious situation than that of Autair Helicopter Services. This case is more serious because when the application was made for a class 4 charter commercial air service with group B aircraft the air transport board declined the application after hearing testimony in Timmins. Incidentally, may I tell the minister that although a motion was passed for the production of the decision of the board, the transcript of the evidence and several other items, I have not received these yet and I hope it will be possible for me to obtain them in due course.
In the case of Georgian Bay Airways Limited, the application was made for a class 4 charter commercial service with group B aircraft and it was declined by the air transport board after the air transport board had given careful consideration, not only to the position of this company in so far as its equipment was concerned but also in so far as its over-all position was concerned.
In this case the minister did not overrule the board. He did worse than that; he changed the law. The minister, by order in council, passed a regulation which amended the law and which allowed Georgian Bay aircraft company to make another application for practically the same service. I would like to refer to the order in council which changed the regulations. It is P.C.60/65 dated January 15, 1960 and the substantive part of the order reads as follows:
The commercial air service regulations are amended by revoking subsection (1) of section 6 and substituting therefor the following:
6. (1) Applicants for licences to operate commercial air services in all classes other than class 1 are exempted from the operation of subsection 3.

of section 15 of the act, provided that in substitution therefor applicants for licences to operate classes 2 and 3, group A of class 4, classes 5 and 6 shall satisfy the board that the proposed commercial air services would be in the public interest.
Until that time an application such as was made by Georgian Bay Airways Limited was controlled by section 15(3) of the Aeronautics Act which reads:
The board shall not issue any such licence unless it is satisfied that the proposed commercial air service is and will be required by the present and future public convenience and necessity.
The air transport board, after hearing evidence at Timmins, came to the conclusion that in the light of the present and future public convenience and necessity the application should not be granted.
My submission is that the minister should have amended the act. He ought not to have allowed this company to enter by the back door, by making an amendment to these regulations, but he should have come forward and amended the Aeronautics Act, stipulating that the present and future public convenience and necessity provision was no longer required to be shown by aircraft companies of this kind, but that in future they need only show proof of public interest if that was the intention. I maintain that when so much has been said by those who sit on the other side of the house about a bill of rights, if there are two methods by which a result can be brought about-and I submit there were not-then at least the least objectionable method is the one which should have been taken.
Again I should like to bring this to the attention of the committee. It is doubtful whether in view of what has been done that the air transport board may not be liable to legal action for having done something by virtue of an order in council which should have been done by virtue of an amendment to a statute. So it seems to me that in this sense the matter is more serious than the Autair case.
The granting of this licence was a circumventing of parliament. It confirms exactly what the air industries and transport association have been saying to the Prime Minister and the government, namely what is the use of having an air transport board if its decisions are to be circumvented, in one case by the minister overruling the board and in the other case by the passing of an order in council which cancels what is contained in the act? It seems to me that this is a direct challenge to the functions of the air transport board, and that the action taken in this case strikes at the very root of parliament.
There are a number of other items which I should like to discuss, but the committee
Supply-Transport
has been generous. I will not proceed further than to mention them. There is the very important question of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence. There have been contradictory statements in this respect. The minister made a statement at Baie Comeau. The Prime Minister made a directly opposite statement at Halifax. I have the statements here and can put them on record. Certainly, the minister made his views perfectly clear in so far as winter navigation was concerned. It was also made quite clear in the speech delivered by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works. I quote from the speech made by the minister to the Dominion Marine Association and the lake carriers association on January 22, 1958:
With this group of ships available it should be possible within the next few years to meet virtually all the requirements in the St. Lawrence and gulf areas including such winter shipping as may wish to proceed to the various ports in the lower St. Lawrence, even as far as Quebec, and in the gulf and Atlantic areas generally.
When this was put to the minister in the course of questions on orders of the day, he interjected: "Up to but not necessarily as far as Quebec."
I wish to place on record in Hansard what the Prime Minister said in Halifax and in Saint John. The right hon. gentleman wanted, surely, to reassure the people of those two ports, and he did reassure them according to the report which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of November 16, 1959, when the following appeared:
He reassured Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick, port officials by saying his government has no plans to keep the St. Lawrence river open in winter. Reports of such a scheme have brought protests from maritime shipping men who say the winter business they depend on may be lost.
Again in the Ottawa Citizen of November 19 the following appeared:
Transport Minister Hees said Tuesday maritime ports have no reason to worry about plans to keep ports along the St. Lawrence north shore open during the winter months.
In fact, he told reporters as he entered a cabinet meeting, north shore communities had told him that they probably would buy their supplies in Saint John or Halifax if their ports are kept open. The maritimes will definitely benefit from this, he said.
I am wondering if this is another case where the government is proceeding without plans or is it simply a matter of prevarication, because there can be no doubt about the minister's statement where he said that winter navigation would be provided, if it were required and necessary, right up to the port of Quebec.
I wish to say just a word about the construction of an additional bridge. Perhaps we can get some explanation of this from the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. He is

Supply-Transport
the hon. gentleman who asked a question in the house one day. I do not think he received a satisfactory reply but there is no doubt about the minister's statement in that respect.
Let me say a final word about the construction of a new bridge between Montreal and the south shore east of the Jacques Cartier bridge. I have on more than one occasion beginning in 1957 referred to a report which is in the Department of Transport entitled "The St. Lawrence Ship Channel and Montreal Harbour Committee of 1950; report on the terms of reference thereof". This is a report which dealt with the construction of facilities in the Montreal harbour and east of that harbour that would have to be undertaken following the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway. The report is a voluminous one. I have only the report dealing with one reference but there are four or five references. Somewhere in this report it is stated that a bridge should be constructed east of the Jacques Cartier bridge linking Montreal and the south shore. I advocated this again in 1958 and saw that sometime afterwards the associate minister of defence had indicated his approval of construction of that nature. In fact, I believe the hon. gentleman went to an association or group in Montreal and said he thought they should make representations for the construction of that bridge.
The point I want to make now is that the minister certainly did not give his colleague very much assistance in that respect when he wrote to the mayors of the municipalities on the south shore. I will not embarrass the minister by putting the correspondence on the record but the minister wrote a letter under date of February 13, 1959 to all of the mayors, the concluding part of which would indicate that regardless of other considerations the course of wisdom for whichever authority might assume responsibility would be to wait at least until the effects of the new Champlain bridge could be examined before undertaking the very substantial financial outlay which would be involved in the construction of yet another bridge.
The minister has in his possession a survey of traffic in Montreal made by traffic experts of the city of Montreal and province of Quebec over the bridges which indicates the probable effect of all of the bridges, the Jacques Cartier bridge, the Victoria bridge and the new Champlain bridge. Notwithstanding that, there are in the city of Montreal, I believe, experts who have come to the conclusion that another bridge is necessary. I know that decisions like this cannot be taken overnight and must be given careful consideration but I urge the minister in the

light of the traffic report which he has received-I guess it is dated 1957-and in the light of the representations which I am sure must have been made to him by many groups and associations in the city of Montreal to give consideration now to the planning and surveying that might be necessary for the construction of an additional bridge east of the Jacques Cartier bridge.
There are other matters with which I should like to deal but I will leave them for consideration as the various items of the department come up during the course of the discussion in this committee.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the hon. member for Laurier whether he would allow me a question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly.
The hon. member has referred to winter navigation. May I ask whether he himself and his party are in favour of winter navigation up to Quebec?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can very easily answer that question, because I have answered it on two previous occasions. The first time was at Quebec, where I had gone to give a talk, and the second was in reply to a question I was asked last winter during our party convention at the Chateau Laurier.
The reply to the question of the hon. member for Charlevoix is as follows: our party is in favour of providing services when they are required to promote industry where necessary, whether it is a matter of supplying icebreakers or other services to promote winter navigation to a port such as Quebec, for instance.
Now, as regards Atlantic ports, in reply to a question by a member from the maritime provinces about Saint John and Halifax harbours, I added that if the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines had accepted my recommendation that an economic study be made of the impact of the St. Lawrence seaway on every part of Canada, we might be in a position to know if the impact on those ports has been favourable or otherwise. And should the results be adverse as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell), and others are inclined to believe, the government could then take proper remedial steps.
However, with regard to winter navigation to the port of Quebec, my party, as the record shows, did everything that the Quebec port authorities had asked for.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask another question of the hon. member, if he does not mind.

speechtext: Order. The Chair recognizes the hon. member for Port Arthur.

I do not want to interfere with the hon. member's questioning but perhaps he will have an opportunity to ask questions later. At times the Minister of Transport strikes me as being a rather gay socialist and at others as a fay free enterpriser. The previous speaker has given an indication as to where these free enterprise instincts have led the minister as far as Autair, T.C.A., and the Georgian Bay commitments are concerned.
I thought the minister was somewhat bland in his outline and in his reference to the fact that his department has shown only a 4 per cent growth. I remember that the hon. member in opposition-forgive me for ever bringing up the way people handle themselves in opposition-urged the previous administration to cut down the growing government service. Now the hon. gentleman's tune has changed. If this scale of growth is across the board we can imagine what will be the size of the civil service if this government remains in power for as long as the previous one.
I expected that the minister might have given us in addition to an outline of the work of his department a review of the transportation picture in Canada. It is in a rather bad snafu. I think this stems from the fact that Canadians cannot and never have been able to make up their minds, just as the minister has not, whether transport is to be an ancillary or a main field of government enterprise. If you want to put it more directly, where should private enterprise fit into the transport picture? I have never been able to see that we have any definite public consensus as to this situation.
I have been following very closely the hearings of the royal commission on transportation. I think the report of their proceedings now covers pretty close to 20,000 pages. The commission has sat throughout the country in the various provinces and has received a tremendous number of briefs. In glancing at the proceedings it is apparent that one can enumerate a tremendous number of transportation problems throughout the country, and it seems to me that with such a vigorous minister, a minister with so much pep and energy and with so much enthusiasm, we might expect more leadership with regard to our transportation problems than we are getting from him or are likely to get from the royal commission.

I think it is fair for me to comment about the royal commision that in the main it has spent most of its time, as a result of the crossexamination by railway counsel and counsel for the western provinces, on the problem of the Crowsnest rates, which is one of the fundamental transportation enigmas in Canada. But when you examine the briefs that have been presented by the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario and the Atlantic provinces you get a picture of our transportation problems that is much broader than merely the Crowsnest rates and, Lord knows, the Crowsnest rates are problem enough.
If we start in the maritimes field we find a wide difference of opinion over the Chignecto canal. There are wide differences of opinion as between Halifax and Saint John and Quebec with respect to the topic mentioned by the previous speaker, winter shipping on the St. Lawrence river. It is apparent from the brief presented by the province of Quebec that that province feels very strongly and intends to insist-one might almost say demand-that the shipping season be extended on the St. Lawrence, and it is also apparent from the scope of the enterprises that are being established and have been established in Labrador that a much longer shipping season is expected out of Seven Islands. What is involved is not only a full ocean shipping season for the transport of ore to the east coast of the United States but also a longer shipping season into the port of Montreal. I have figures here indicating that the difference between the cost of goods landed at Halifax or Saint John and shipped westward into Upper Canada, as the maritimers say, and goods landed at Montreal is on the average somewhere between $12 and $16 a ton. This indicates to me a rather enormous potential saving for shippers and the economy.
But against this the minister has to balance, as we do, the effect on the maritime ports that would result from encouraging the transfer of shipments to Montreal. This is one of the very large issues in the eastern part of Canada into which the development of the Chignecto canal and even the causeway to Prince Edward Island perhaps fit. It is something that indicates the turmoil in our transportation situation at the present time and the need for clear leadership.
I agree with the hon. member for Laurier that there seems to be a contradiction in the policy or what masquerades as the policy of the government with respect to winter ship-talking to an engineer who is familiar with ping on the St. Lawrence. I gather from the Montreal harbour situation that if sufficient research were put into the matter it might be possible to do something about preventing at least for the month of December

Supply-Transport
and perhaps lor another month early in the spring the building up ol ice from the bottom that takes place in the channels of Montreal harbour and really chokes off the shipping season sooner than one might expect. If that particular problem could be prevented in the stretch of water up as far as Montreal harbour there would certainly seem to be no reason why we should not be considering not only winter shipping into Quebec city but winter shipping into Montreal. I think we have to realize that until some real revolution in technology occurs the locks up river from Montreal are not going to be open for any longer period.
With regard to the general transportation problems of the province of Quebec, the Hon. Mr. Johnson, who presented the Quebec brief to the royal commission on transportation, was very forthright in his demands and requests for a whole host of things in terms of transportation services. He ranged all the way from insisting that the signs at Dorval airport should be in both languages to the argument that it was unfair that the Ontario Northland railway happened to tap part of Quebec. He went further and argued that the railway building policy of the government of Canada had not been fair to Quebec and he had a number of statistical analyses showing that development by the railways of Canada had resulted in less mileage per capita in Quebec than anywhere else.
He followed up this argument, which I personally could not appreciate, with something that I could appreciate, the need of a more forthright developmental policy by the railways in opening up Quebec's resources. Before he finished he went so far as to say that if the federal government would not give aid the province would not hesitate at all to jump into the field with truck highways or railroads.
When we come to the submissions of the province of Ontario we find that in the main the brief is a very extreme criticism of the Canadian railways. The point is made repeatedly that the province of Ontario is not satisfied with the railway services it has got. The opinion is expressed very strongly that the reason highway development and truck transportation have advanced as much as they have is that the railways have not given the service that they should, that they have become decadent industries in a dynamic economy. Again this is something that I personally cannot quite swallow but it emphasizes what has become a fairly popular view about our railway problems in Canada.
Again, the tragedies in terms of employment that have occurred on the railways, the dislocation of the labour force, the shifting

of the labour force, the problems at Stratford and London about which the minister has been probed, indicate that all is not well within this field and that we need forthright leadership. I hope the minister noted that the report of the parliamentary committee on the government railways contained one very succinct paragraph indicating strong dissatisfaction with the role played by Canadian National Railways in its public relations with the communities that the railway services. I think the minister has to do a job of interpreting that paragraph to the Canadian National management because one of the most serious of all employment problems, one that fits into the transportation picture, is the great cut-back that has taken place and is going to take place in the railway labour force. There is a need for the very best of relations between the railways, the unions and the communities involved to see that this is done in as fair a way as possible.
We would suggest to the minister that he should be in a position to outline to us what the government accepts as its responsibility in so far as this dislocation is concerned. He probably knows that at the present time the responsibility is diffuse. The province accepts some responsibility and the Department of Labour accepts some but we are not sure where the railways stand. They have agreements with the unions that are not particularly clear, and it seems to me that the minister could play a much larger role than he has. I think he should be embarrassed by the part he has played in situations such as the London one where all he did was to get up and say that the president of the C.N.R. had refused to meet a delegation or that the C.N.R. did not feel it could consider this matter at the present time.
I could interject here, Mr. Chairman, and say that the minister has a great predilection to concentrate his interests, his public speeches, his optimism, upon the air service side of transportation. We have a total picture of transportation in Canada into which the government has been feet first for a long time. We have pipe lines, air transportation, highway transportation, water transportation and canals, in addition to air services. If the railway situation, in economic terms, has become decadent, if we have an over-mature or declining industry, then it seems to me, and I think the minister knows this, that it raises very real problems in so far as the dislocation of the labour force is concerned.

Might I just point out something to the hon. member. I know there is a municipality in his own riding, I believe, the municipality of Sioux Lookout, which had a

problem that the hon. member for Port Arthur brought to my attention. I had the Canadian National officials go there for a special meeting with the town council of Sioux Lookout, and as a result of that a very satisfactory arrangement was worked out. I received a very nice letter from the mayor of Sioux Lookout which told me how pleased he was with the situation.
I made a special request of the president of the Canadian National, even after they had completed their examination of the London situation. A complete re-examination of the whole situation was made from top to bottom but unfortunately they could not come to any different conclusion. However, this was not through lack of effort on my part or interest on my part, and nothing could be done to change the decision.

I thank the minister, but Sioux Lookout is just outside my constituency. I am interested in it because it was my birthplace. I agree that the compromise arrangement is satisfactory in the short term, but what I have been trying to suggest to the minister has been that there is a much larger problem here. Who is responsible, for example, for the decline or the complete disruption of communities? I am not suggesting that the government should be, but the government has accepted a special responsibility in the Elliot Lake and the Bancroft situations. What is the responsibility in so far as railway problems are concerned?
If automation is having this grave effect, as we can see it is, in the transportation industry, surely this should be a matter of concern to more than the Minister of Labour. I would suggest that it should be a very real problem for the Minister of Transport, if he is indeed in charge or his department is in charge of the over-all transportation policy for the country. You not only have to look at the dynamic part of transportation, such as jets flying faster and runways getting longer, but also at the slipping, declining parts of the transportation picture.
When you look at the situation in northwestern Ontario or northern Ontario-I thinir the minister is aware that one could go on for a very long time in so far as transportation is concerned-you can give some examples of situations about which the people are not satisfied. We are not satisfied with the way the work is progressing at the lakehead terminals. This is only indirectly connected with the minister's department since the Minister of Public Works has to bear major responsibility. The discontent is more than local. This discontent spreads over the prairies because the farmers expected so

Supply-Transport
much more from the seaway than was actually experienced. Whether it is true or false, there is a belief that this government and the previous government had not prepared facilities for helping us to compete with Duluth and the other United States ports. My own feeling is that this mood is exaggerated, but here again we have not had a clear policy integrating this problem with the highway situation and the railways with any developments that they are going to make in the lakehead terminals.
The minister is aware of the fact that the western provinces and the cities of the lake-head were so disturbed about the situation they formed a special port association with the idea of promoting the whole affair and developing more policies. This again indicates that there has been a vacuum or something close to a vacuum in the minister's department in not having an over-all policy laid down in this connection that was readily understandable. Surely when you have communities such as these that are relatively isolated, that are in a dudgeon and worked up about a number of things in this transportation picture, it indicates a lack of clarity on the part of the senior administrative agency. I would suggest to the minister that his department is responsible.
I have recently drawn to his attention complaints about icebreaking. The prairie farmers think it is important, and the lakehead communities think it is important in terms of employment that the elevators have boats at them as early as possible in the spring, and that the boats are able to get service from these elevators as late as possible in the fall. I have had accusations made at the lake-head to the effect that both the prairie farmers and the lakehead people were let down by the icebreaker service this year when the Alexander Henry was pulled out of the harbour prematurely. The ironical part of the situation is that the president of the lakehead harbour commission appointed by the minister-we will assume he is a good Conservative, and in any event he is a fine man is the head of a particular elevator. His elevator had to wait 12 days after the opening of shipping, according to the information I have, before a ship was able to get to the dock and get any grain out of that very large elevator. The reason was that the government icebreaker had not bothered to go to that particular elevator to open it up for shipping. We see, therefore, that even the minister's own friends suffered from this action.
We have a shipyard at the lakehead, and this is another aspect of the over-all transportation picture that is most unsatisfactory.

Supply-Transport
There were all these dreams sponsored by the present minister for external affairs and the Minister of Transport himself when in opposition, that when the Conservative millennium came-that would be immediately after the election-we would have a salt water fleet in being, and have a great expansion in this particular field. All I know is that our particular shipyard has not built anything of substance for a long time. I know that the shipyards in British Columbia are in a bad way and that the shipyard at Collingwood is within sight of the end of its orders. We have a depressed industry, again in this vitally important part of the transportation picture. I know the minister has given encouragement where he could by awarding contracts here and there for relatively minor craft, but the fact remains that in this aspect of the transportation picture Canada has no fleet. Where is our salt water fleet?
Again we find we have not the kind of leadership we expected from this particular department. When you get to the prairies, in so far as the transportation picture is concerned we find there are still complaints about the meteorological service provided by the department. This is in the agricultural field, so I suppose there will be western members speaking about that.
However, I should like to return to the problem with which the royal commission has been preoccupied, that is the freight rate structure and the Crowsnest pass rates. What is going to be the solution for the dilemma of the subsidy picture? I think we are entitled to know how the minister plans to handle the situation that is developing between the railways and the unions which are now in negotiation. The conciliation stage has been reached. We not only have the situation that any award to the unions will put the railways in a more difficult position, but we may have a strike. We also have the situation where the $20 million subsidy is beginning to come to an end. This is the minister's responsibilty. He fathered the bill in the house, took it into committee, brought it back and we approved it. Then $20 million was pumped into the freight rate structure of Canada. This amount was allocated for one year and that year is almost up.
The royal commission on transportation which was to give us some kind of solution to this particular problem has set up hearings for next October. If that commission comes up with any kind of substantial report many more months will ensue. Where are we going to go with the $20 million subsidy? What is the interim measure we can count on from this government to ease the burden upon the 
shippers or are they going to allow the rates to go back up to the 17 per cent picture?
Before I leave the Crowsnest rates may I say that it seems to me that the government has given us a regrettable lack of leadership and direction in this particular field. The Prime Minister gave the assurance in the house before the commission was appointed that the Crowsnest rates, in so far as the agreement was concerned, would not be touched. I think that is the kind of commitment we can understand. But this leaves the only alternative, it seems to me, of some kind of Chinese face-saving device so that the agreement does not completely lapse for the C.P.R. and then something is going to come from the taxpayers' pocket; I refer to the general taxpayers. That seems to be the only solution. That is really the basic argument underlying the royal commission on transportation.
It seems to me that we shall never clear up one of the biggest problems of the transport picture until we get leadership from this government on two things. One is a final solution, even if it must be spread over a number of years, for the grain carrying dilemmas of the railways. The second is some formula by which the railway workers' wages can be arrived at. As long as the railways are going to be controlled and regulated there must be some formula that is accepted by the nation as a whole on which these wages can find a parity.
Again we get no indication that the government is working in a leadership way to develop such a formula. It is leaving it to the normal channels which I would agree are perfectly sound in most industries. I refer to the contest between labour and management. But this is not a proper kind of contest when you have the railways so regulated as they are by the board of transport commissioners and vulnerable to decisions of this particular parliament in so far as grain rates are concerned.
I do not know whether the white goods formula is the one that needs to be transferred to the railway industry to determine the wage structure but I certainly feel that we have every right to expect leadership from the minister in developing a wage formula set-up for the railways. Despite the relationship that I or my political party might have, I would even go so far as to suggest that this formula should come no matter what management may feel about it and no matter what labour may feel about it. We need to get a working formula in this field. I am not going to suggest to the minister what it should be but I certainly suggest to him and

his department that he should be developing this policy and making it part of the public view and the public discussion, in fairness to all parties in the partnership.
As to British Columbia, we have a British Columbian in our party who will touch on what appears to be one of the fundamental transportation problems in British Columbia, namely the famed Kettle Valley railway. I know this is a vital part of the minister's responsibility. But the other aspect of the British Columbia picture that fits into the railway transportation is the long problem that province has had since confederation to get its products into the eastern Canadian market at some kind of competitive position.
It is obvious from the submission that British Columbia again has made to the royal commission on transportation that they are not satisfied. I know that one of the dilemmas here is that if you give too many concessions to British Columbia to put their goods into the eastern Canadian market, it means that they can cut the throats of suppliers much closer at hand who also have the same type of products. I am thinking in terms of fruit and lumber and situations like that. I do not know what the way out of that particular dilemma is but I certainly know that it is a large enough and strong enough issue that we need some indication from the government of what it plans to do.
One of the things we expected from the minister this session was changes in the Canada Shipping Act. I still do not know whether we are going to get them. I thought he might let us know what the situation is in so far as United States progress is concerned under their particular act, and whether he is really ready at this time to give us these changes. I know that the basic problem here is that we have never had explained fully in Canada why the head of the United States coastguard takes a so much stronger view of safety than does the minister's own department. Why is it that the admiral in charge of the United States coastguard is so strongly against the opening up of licensing to foreign ships in comparison to the lengths to which the Canadian government will go? The minister's department is quite prepared to license foreign captains and mates for navigation in the lakes and to go much further than, as I understand it, the admiral is willing to go. Why is it that this department puts a so much smaller premium on safety than does the United States coastguard? I do not think we can assume that the admiral is a fool. I think we are aware of the fact that a number of accidents are taking place in the lakes. There was a serious one in the lakes just
Supply-Transport
a few days ago in which foreign ships were involved. It seems to me that we might expect something in this particular field from the minister.
The minister gave us a survey not too long ago of what his government and the department were doing with regard to harbours. I was interested that one of the hon. members on the government side rose in his place and touted some harbours on down the lake from Oshawa. I think Oshawa is extremely lucky to have a minister in the cabinet to get the benefit of the act and the development that it is probably going to get. But the unexplained part of the minister's sermon to me is an explanation over-all as to just how this developing harbour picture along the lakes is going to fit into the overall economic development. I think we are entitled to ask this question because one of the great expectations really up until last fall was that the lakes would become open to foreign shipping and there was a real doubt that our own domestic shipping was going to be able to survive.
The minister went to Windsor last November, I believe, and gave a speech which was really an indicator that his department felt that lake shipping was going to be more than able to hold its own against foreign shipping; in other words, that there was not going to be the revolutionary switch that so many people had counted upon. This indicates that a good deal of the dreaming and many of the grandiose plans-and I think some of the dreaming and the grandiose stuff was encouraged by the hon. member for Laurier- are not coming to fruition and are most unlikely to do so. This raises in my mind the question as to how accurate these surveys may be; what are the norms or the standards that these surveys crews are taking in judging the potential both of the harbour and the hinterland of the harbour; the way it can fit in with competing harbours along the way and the whole national growth. I can underline this matter for the minister by saying how relatively disappointed the people in our part of the country and the west have been over the failure of the opening of the seaway last year to generate more traffic than it did.
A lot of people are still dissatisfied with the Welland canal tolls. Here again is another transportation problem which is still a very live topic.

The Welland canal situation is still an issue so far as tolls are concerned. The minister may think it is a dead issue but he is still getting briefs and representations. There is dissatisfaction in the west with the tolls structure, and I think here again we could expect more in the way of a final solution to the dissatisfaction over the toll structure on the Welland canal.
I would also welcome it very much if the minister later in the estimates would give us a picture of the expenditures that the United States is making along the Detroit section of the seaway, and also at Sault Ste. Marie so far as the deepening of the canal there is concerned. It certainly seems to me that when the United States is finally faced with the total cost of what they are putting up so far as the seaway is concerned, we may have opened up another argumentative chapter in the Welland canal tolls. It certainly does not make sense to me that they should deepen the Sault Ste Marie canal to the depth of the Welland canal and not expect some return from Canada. I am wondering if that return might possibly be a dropping of the tolls of the Welland canal, which as I understand it go right to the Canadian government and to no other. We hope to have the opportunity later on in the estimates to go into almost every phase of the department's activities and we look forward to seeing the minister and his friendly presence with us for many more days.

Would the hon. member permit a question. I was interested in his remarks with regard to the Crowsnest pass rates. I wondered if the C.C.F. policy was that they would advocate scrapping these rates; but I understand he would let us down years. Is this the C.C.F.'s policy at the moment?

I should like to remind the hon. member that I am not that big a sucker. What I was suggesting was that both the railways and the western provinces are focussing attention on the Crowsnest pass rates before the royal commission on transportation. It seems to me that this is just one part of the railway problem.
Personally I and most of my associates are not frightened by the word "subsidy" or "subvention". We know that what is going to come out of the situation, whether the agreement lasts or not, is that somehow the railways are going to be given more money.

All I was suggesting was some kind of realistic leadership from our political leaders rather than leaving it to be thrashed out ad nauseam before the royal commission. It seems to me we have had a failure of political leadership by the government in not solving this situation.
If the hon. member would like to know my recommendations in this regard they are to find out what the cost differentiation is between hauling the grain and what is actually received then some kind of formula for over the years could be prepared to see that the money comes back to the railways as far as the difference is concerned.
Order.
Having said that, I think the hon. member knows that this cost difference is very debatable. I notice someone is calling order. I believe I have the right-
You have made your speech.

I understand, Mr. Chairman, that in committee once someone else has got to his feet and made an interjection one can carry on for another half an hour. However, I do not intend to do that; that is all I have to say.

Mr. Chairman, nowhere else is the Minister of Transport's department so important than in my part of the country. Consequently I want to deal in general with certain aspects of the minister's department. I am thinking specifically of the marine services, the Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines and the hotel services of the Canadian National Railways.
The principal reason, a very important one, why we consider the minister's department so important to our part of the country is that we are a province largely undeveloped from the point of view of transportation. We still do not have the services of a trans-Canada highway across our province. We still depend largely on the Canadian National Railways to transport our goods from east to west; and we are dependent on the marine services of the minister's department, including the steamship services of the Canadian National Railways, as a vital source of supply around our coast line.
We were very happy last year to see the arrival of two new icebreakers to be based at St. John's. I might say that these icebreakers are largely the result of the great personal interest the minister has taken in our part of the country and I wish to thank him for that at this moment. However, the arrival of these two icebreakers did succeed in focussing attention on a problem which I feel necessary to bring to his attention, and that is the rates of pay of seamen employed on the department's vessels.

It has been brought to my attention that seamen in the Newfoundland agency of the minister's department receive less pay than their counterparts in the Nova Scotia agency or the Prince Edward Island agency of the minister's department; and the maritime seamen receive less pay than their counterparts in the Quebec agencies. These men are doing similar work and of times are working side by side, yet their rates of pay vary and I am sorry to say very considerably. I think consideration should certainly be given to equalizing the rates of pay of these men doing similar work under similar conditions who are carrying out a very vital and necessary role in the life and trade of this nation.
The second point I would draw to the attention of the committee is under the heading of the Canadian National Railways. This is a subject I have brought to the minister's attention in previous sessions during the passage of his estimates. I refer specifically to the necessity for enlarging the Canadian National Railways Newfoundland hotel at St. John's. I believe, although I do not have the facts to back up this contention, that the Newfoundland hotel is one of the few C.N.R. hotels across Canada that actually makes a profit.
I have some very interesting figures I would like to place on record with regard to hotel accommodation. The latest available figures-[DOT] my source is the dominion bureau of statistics -indicate that Newfoundland is far behind other provinces in Canada in hotel accommodation. I realize that the minister will say this is not solely his responsibility and that he would expect free enterprise to move in and fill this gap; but when free enterprise fails to move in then I think it is his responsibility. I think specifically of Canadian National Railways.
For example, in the city of St. John's there is one major hotel-the C.N.R. Newfoundland hotel-and four small hotels with a total of 405 beds for a metropolitan city of well over 80,000 population. The city of Saint John, New Brunswick, a city of comparable size, has six hotels, with a total accommodation of 1,013. It is interesting to note that the city of Halifax which has recently had an addition made to its C.N.R. hotel, the Nova Scotian hotel, has more beds, more hotel accommodation, than the whole province of Newfoundland. I say this to underline the necessity of the Canadian National Railways making a substantial increase in the accommodation available in the Newfoundland hotel. I think sound business principles would dictate that this be done, because anyone who has had the experience of travelling through St. John's knows that this hotel is constantly
Supply-Transport
overcrowded and that one can rarely get in there. I believe the Newfoundland board of trade has brought this subject to the attention of the minister on several occasions and I hope when the minister again brings in his estimates he will be able to report that this important hotel is substantially larger than it is today.
The other matter I wish to direct to the attention of the minister at this time is the necessity of an alternative airstrip to the St. John's airport. The hon. gentleman officiated at the official opening of the magnificent new terminal at St. John's a little over a year ago. However, I am sure that he, like many other hon. members, has the experience of travelling by air in this part of the country. He knows that this is an area where flying is often hampered by dense fog and where weather conditions generally are uncertain. It happens on occasions that the airport is closed in for considerable length of time. Only a few weeks ago it was closed for eight or nine days. This necessitated the use of air facilities at Argentia, which is 90 miles out of St. John's. Passengers leaving by T.C.A. had to be transported 90 miles over secondary roads before they could get to the air carriers 90 miles away.
Were Trans-Canada Air Lines to agree to providing an alternative airstrip they would find an ideal location about 20 miles from St. John's, an area which is virtually fog free all the year round. At any rate it has longer periods of clear visibility than the particular area where the St. John's airport is located. I am thinking of the general area from 18 to 30 miles outside the city on the trans-Canada highway, a good paved road. This would be an ideal location for an alternative airstrip. I believe repeated representations have been made to the minister's department by various organizations in Newfoundland, including the board of trade, with regard to this matter, in addition to representations from members of the travelling public.
There is one last question I wish to raise, and it concerns a matter which is vital to all of us in that part of Canada. I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite will agree. I am referring to the need for the provision of an east coast ferry. As I have pointed out, the trans-Canada highway across our province will not be completed for perhaps another ten years at the rate we are going. The advantages of a ferry service between eastern Newfoundland and the mainland of Canada are too numerous to mention here. It would certainly lead to a great influx of tourists to the most populated part of the province, namely the Avalon peninsula where almost two thirds of

Supply-Transport
our population live. As things stand now, the ferry William Carson is fulfilling a vital role. Nevertheless, it is located on the extreme eastern end of the island, and until the trans-Canada highway is completed this ferry is virtually useless to the vast majority of the population. I might say to the minister that even when the trans-Canada highway is completed I think he will have to give consideration to establishing another ferry from the west coast. In any event, I would ask that the minister take this matter into consideration. I shall have further questions of a more specific nature to ask when the relevant items come up for consideration.

The estimates of the department of the Minister of Transport are always awaited with great interest by myself and by many of the people of my constituency, because in my constituency of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador there are two of the largest airports in the world, Goose and Gander.
The northern part of the island depends on the minister's department for its communications. I speak of the Labrador coast where radiotelephones and communications are part of the minister's responsibilities. I am thinking also of the services of the C.N.R. which are so important to northern Newfoundland and the coast of Labrador and which, again, come under the minister's jurisdiction.
Before talking about some of the things which particularly affect my riding I should like to refer to remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for St. John's East. I noted what the hon. member said regarding the need for another airstrip to supplement Torbay. As a matter of fact, I happen to be one of the passengers to whom he referred as having had to drive 90 miles from St. John's in order to board a T.C.A. flight at Argentia. I certainly endorse the hon. member's suggestion that an alternate airstrip be provided for use in the case of bad weather at Torbay.
The hon. member also mentioned the need for a new ferry. Certainly that is something with which we can all agree wholeheartedly. As to his comment about the trans-Canada highway not being finished for 10 years, it is true that if the present administration remains in power for that long it is going to take a long time to finish the trans-Canada highway, but with the change in government that has to come the trans-Canada highway is bound to go forward much quicker under the more liberal arrangements which will be made with the Atlantic provinces by the future Liberal government.

There was a small omission in the remarks of the hon. member for St. John's East which I should like to bring to his attention. As a matter of fact I had intended to get in touch with him about this so that he might use his influence with the Minister of Transport. My point is this: in the wintertime, particularly after a heavy snowfall, the road to the Torbay airport is frequently not ploughed properly simply because there is a small section of the road which the city says the airport should plough, and which the Department of Transport says the city should plough. On one occasion last winter the road was ploughed, shovelled or opened by someone to the width of one car. The result was that when the planes did come in after the snowfall and traffic began to accumulate at the airport, a traffic jam developed and the cars were unable to pass in either direction and the passengers had to walk. I happen, Mr. Chairman, to be a constituent of the hon. member for St. John's East.
You have an excellent member.
As one of his constituents I am going to make an appeal to him. Some might say that my political philosophy and that of the hon. member for St. John's East are not the same and that is true-
Oh, I don't know.

-but let me say that I have some constituents-very few fortunately- who do not agree with the party I represent and I would expect the same treatment from my member as I accord to those constituents of mine who through faulty judgment fail to support me.
Let me now return from a discussion of the problems of my member to a discussion of the problems of my own constituents. I should like to talk to the Minister of Transport about the needs of the town of Gander. I am fortunate in the respect that I believe the minister knows this town very well. As a matter of fact, the minister was so interested in the town that he paid it a visit during the winter of 1958 when Gander was not at its best and travelling could not have been particularly comfortable. Nevertheless the minister did visit Gander during that winter and explained in a conversation there, I believe, that should his government be returned to power Gander would go up and up and up. It is in connection with Gander's future that I want to talk particularly and I am very glad that the minister has seen Gander both in the winter and again since under more pleasant and less contentious circumstances. I am always glad to welcome the Minister of Transport to my constituency.

There has been, I think understandably, quite a bit of concern on the part of the people of Gander as to its future in the jet age. Gander is probably the best example of a town created by the modern age of air travel. Gander is truly a product of the air age. It has today a beautiful modern townsite with lovely homes, one of the very best air terminals in the world and all the paraphernalia that makes for good living in a modern town including up to date schools and fine churches. Everything there depends for its sustenance and its future on what happens to Gander as an airport.
Before proceeding I should like to suggest to the minister that perhaps during the discussion of his estimates or at least before the session ends he might find it convenient to make a statement as to what he thinks the future holds for Gander. I am personally satisfied that the future of Gander is assured. We are now just entering the air age. The large number of air passengers travelling now will surely have increased tremendously, let us say 10 years from now. I read with interest an article appearing in the May issue of Flying, a widely read aviation magazine which deals with the future of air travel and the coming passenger boom in the world's airlines which would have a definite effect on Gander. The article states in part:
American spending on foreign travel in 1950 was $1,200 million: it should double that and more in this year of 1960.
I do not have time to refer to the arguments the author uses to support his contention. The article continues:
But for the air alone-and only in terms of those countries outside the U.S.S.R. and China, who report regularly to the international civil aviation organization-the curve of world scheduled passenger traffic may well go from an estimated 104 million passengers this year to about 186 million in 1970. These totals cover both domestic and international travel. Assuming that the proportionate share of international travel may increase during the decade, the volume of foreign touring by scheduled airline in 1970 may well be more than 50 million passengers per year, as compared with about 19 million today.
Another article in the same issue points out that 175,000 passengers participated in mass passenger transportation by chartered aircraft on transatlantic flights alone. With the huge increase in passenger traffic I cannot see how the modern jet plane alone will be able to account for all of it. The piston and the smaller turboprop planes will participate in this traffic. We cannot overlook the fact, however, that jet travel is increasing and becoming cheaper for the average passenger. If Gander is to compete successfully in this changing air age it will need a longer runway than it has at present. I wish to make a special appeal to the minister in this regard.

As I said before, the airport at Gander represents a large investment both by the people and the government. I am sure the minister is interested in the future of Gander from both the standpoint of humanity and the standpoint of the heavy investment which the government has made in it. If Gander is to become a real jet airport it must have the facilities to handle modern jet aircraft. Gander has the best terminal building in North America. The communications facilities there are second to none in the world. The Gander oceanic air traffic control facility with its accompanying approach control facility and tower control facility are of a very high order. Gander has the latest instrument approach control system and an instrument landing system. The snow clearing facilities for the winter operation are among the best certainly on this continent if not in the world. For example, during the month of March this year the total snowfall for Gander was in excess of 65 inches yet the airport was not closed for any period in spite of this record amount of snow. What Gander does lack is a jet runway.
The longest runway at Gander is 8,600 feet. We require a minimum of 9,600 feet or in round figures 10,000 feet. The runway length presents a problem to the pilot. For example, when a pilot is landing under instrument control it may be that his approach is a little higher than normal or his speed may be somewhat faster than normal.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was recounting the splendid facilities at Gander airport. It has practically everything a modem airport needs in the way of facilities to look after aircraft landing in almost all kinds of weather. I was pointing out, however, that a longer runway is necessary if Gander is really to continue its important place in aviation during the jet age. I pointed out that the longest runway at Gander was 8,600 feet and that a runway approximately 10,000 feet long is necessary today.
For example, when a pilot is landing under instrument control he may come in a little high and fast. Normally that may not matter but if in bad weather and difficult conditions he has a long runway on which to land he is going to feel much more confident and will

Supply-Transport
make a landing when otherwise under marginal circumstances he might decide he had to go elsewhere. This is particularly important today when jets are in general use. If the investment at Gander is to be protected and if the people Who live at Gander are to have a reasonably secure future it is most necessary that a longer runway be provided.
Many of the aircraft operating through Gander are en route to or from Europe and for operational reasons the pilot has to make up his mind whether he will land at Gander or choose an alternative airport. The length of the runway definitely would be a factor in his mind. The fact that the jet age is not passing Gander by is very well illustrated by the fact that every week a number of jet aircraft land at Gander even with the handicap of what for these times is a comparatively short runway. I would ask the minister to ascertain how many of the larger jet aircraft use Gander at the present time.
Another good reason for the belief that Gander will continue to be used is the amount of freight that is handled there. Last Saturday, I believe, one of the large international airlines shipped 50,000 pounds of lobster and before the season is over they hope to ship a total of 800,000 pounds. That is one commodity alone which is being shipped from Gander. If my understanding is correct, air freight will play a very important part in commercial aviation in the future. As a matter of fact, it seems quite evident that the air transportation of passengers and freight is bound to grow enormously during the next few years. With this in mind it would seem to be a logical step to provide the great airport at Gander with one or, if possible, two runways adequate in length to handle the type of aircraft now coming into general use.
For a few minutes I should like to talk about communications on the Labrador coast. The coast of Labrador depends upon the Department of Transport for its radio communications system. The small settlements along the Labrador coast depend on radiotelephone sets for communication with the outside world. I have mentioned this matter on various occasions before. Communications on the Labrador coast are one of the matters which the Department of Transport inherited at the time of confederation. Truly the places are small and a comparatively small proportion of the population of Canada is involved, but nevertheless their problem is a real one. I would ask the minister to consider providing radiotelephones for Batteau, Williams Harbour,

Georges Cove, Fishing Ships Harbour, Spotted Island, Separation Point and Paradise.
These radiotelephone sets are small and comparatively inexpensive but their importance is very great. Their value is far out of proportion to their cost. As I have said, the communications system, through inheritance, is one of the services to be provided by the Department of Transport and I hope that in the near future these communities which are without radiotelephone sets will be provided with them. May I repeat that the cost is small but the value to the people concerned is exceedingly great. These sets may mean the difference between life and death, particularly during the long winter when the coast of Labrador is locked up tight.
With regard to airstrips, I should like to mention St. Anthony. The provincial government spent some money to develop a small airstrip at St. Anthony, one at North West River and one at Nain. Those at St. Anthony and North West River need money spent on them so that they can better handle planes particularly during the freeze-up and breakup periods. Again the amount of money required is not great but the need is most urgent. This is particularly so because these small airstrips will provide a means of communication with the hospitals on the Labrador coast and also will provide a means of transportation all year round for the people who live in these remote areas.
I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for St. John's East, in extending thanks to the minister for the icebreakers which have been serving a useful purpose in Newfoundland, especially in places in my riding like Botwood, Lewisporte and others. These places are deeply appreciative of the service of these icebreakers now located in Newfoundland.
Before I sit down, I should like to pay tribute to the officers and crews of the Canadian National coastal steamers which operate in Newfoundland waters. Naturally I am thinking of those that operate in my own district which extends from the central part of Newfoundland or which from a marine viewpoint, extend along the coast from Notre Dame bay to the northernmost part of Labrador. The crews of these ships are carrying on a very great service in the tradition of those seamen who for generations have served the coast of Newfoundland. In some parts of Newfoundland today other means of transportation are supplanting or supplementing the coastal steamer, but in northern areas the coastal steamer is extremely vital. These men are carrying on, as I said, in the great tradition of the crews of

such ships as the Glencoe, the Sagona, the Prospero and the Caribou, and they are doing so today in ships like the Nonia, the Springdale, the Burgeo and the Northern Ranger. These seamen are carrying out their work efficiently, with courtesy and kindliness and, above all, with a splendid sense of duty.
In conclusion I should like to go back to the question of Gander and ask if the minister could not find it possible to make a statement which will clarify what is likely to be the future of this important airport town.

I do not intend to take up very much time of the committee tonight, but I thought I should say a few words about air travel particularly because of its importance to Edmonton. Our new international airport at Edmonton is now at the stage where its runways, taxi strips and aprons are about finished and there appears to be a good possibility there will be air service out of that airport by the latter part of this year. I can assure the minister that we appreciate the thoughtfulness of his department in making sure that the original plans were changed in order that we might have runways built that would accommodate the largest and fastest long range planes that will be coming to Edmonton as a result of its position as the crossroads of the north. We have been playing a very important part in this field for years. I want to say that we appreciate the fact we will have a new airport which will assure we will be able to continue to play a very important part in long range air travel.
I am wondering a little bit tonight, however, about the local services. At the present time we have a very good T.C.A. service from Edmonton to Calgary. These two cities are less than 200 miles apart and, for years, Edmonton has had the good fortune of having a good city airport in the middle of the city. Its runways are not long enough to accommodate the modern fast transports, but they can accommodate the Viscount type of plane. The flight from Edmonton to Calgary takes about 45 minutes, and you are in the centre of the city within five minutes after getting off the plane. There are half a dozen such flights back and forth every day which accommodate a lot of people. We have a lot of businessmen out there with a lot of hustle who appreciate being able to do a day's work in another city and get back in the evening. Our new international airport is about 20 miles out of town and, depending on traffic conditions, this could mean a trip by taxi or limousine service of from half an hour to 45 minutes longer. A journey of this length by taxi is not much in relation to the long trips by air coast to coast or intercontinental 79951-0-282J
Supply-Transport
but in relation to a flight of 45 minutes duration the possibility of adding a 45-minute taxi trip is one that causes a little disquietude.
There has been no announcement by T.CA.. that they intend to discontinue the flights into the centre of Edmonton. On the other hand, they have not announced that they will continue to give service both to the new international airport and the one in the centre of the city. I think there are passengers for both, and I think both could be paying trips. I am hoping that T.C.A., when the time comes to move some of these facilities from the centre of Edmonton out to the international airport will not move them all. I hope we will still be able to have this quick trip to the very centre of the city of Edmonton.
There is a second aspect to this matter. I feel that the advantages in having an airport in the centre of the city are very great. I believe we are just starting that part of the air age in which vertical take-off flights and short run take-off flights will be coming to the fore. I feel it would be extremely hard to replace this airport. We hardly know or fully appreciate the value it may prove to be in the future. If there were to be a discontinuance of the operation of any major air line into our city centre airport this might weaken our arguments for the retention of that airport. There are other air lines such as C.P.A. and P.W.A. that are presently using this airport. I hope that T.C.A. does not set an example by moving its entire facilities out to the other airport.
I should like to say one more word about the new airport. The plans I have seen for the administration building at the new international airport indicate that it will be a credit, not only to the airport but to the country. Since Edmonton has been the northern centre for air transport for years, and since we have had many of the old bush pilots operating out of Edmonton who have done so much to open up the north and who have done so much for air travel in Canada throughout the years, it is hoped we could make a little gesture in memory of some of our air pioneers. There are plans for a plaque which they would like to have erected. I have brought to the attention of the minister a very suitable, large-sized wall space which I feel would be ideal for a mural. I hope that the small extra cost that might be entailed in making something really worth while and decorative out of that wall space will not deter the department from giving serious consideration to making this gesture to those who have done so much.
