As I said before, the airport at Gander represents a large investment both by the people and the government. I am sure the minister is interested in the future of Gander from both the standpoint of humanity and the standpoint of the heavy investment which the government has made in it. If Gander is to become a real jet airport it must have the facilities to handle modern jet aircraft. Gander has the best terminal building in North America. The communications facilities there are second to none in the world. The Gander oceanic air traffic control facility with its accompanying approach control facility and tower control facility are of a very high order. Gander has the latest instrument approach control system and an instrument landing system. The snow clearing facilities for the winter operation are among the best certainly on this continent if not in the world. For example, during the month of March this year the total snowfall for Gander was in excess of 65 inches yet the airport was not closed for any period in spite of this record amount of snow. What Gander does lack is a jet runway.
The longest runway at Gander is 8,600 feet. We require a minimum of 9,600 feet or in round figures 10,000 feet. The runway length presents a problem to the pilot. For example, when a pilot is landing under instrument control it may be that his approach is a little higher than normal or his speed may be somewhat faster than normal.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was recounting the splendid facilities at Gander airport. It has practically everything a modem airport needs in the way of facilities to look after aircraft landing in almost all kinds of weather. I was pointing out, however, that a longer runway is necessary if Gander is really to continue its important place in aviation during the jet age. I pointed out that the longest runway at Gander was 8,600 feet and that a runway approximately 10,000 feet long is necessary today.
For example, when a pilot is landing under instrument control he may come in a little high and fast. Normally that may not matter but if in bad weather and difficult conditions he has a long runway on which to land he is going to feel much more confident and will

Supply-Transport
make a landing when otherwise under marginal circumstances he might decide he had to go elsewhere. This is particularly important today when jets are in general use. If the investment at Gander is to be protected and if the people Who live at Gander are to have a reasonably secure future it is most necessary that a longer runway be provided.
Many of the aircraft operating through Gander are en route to or from Europe and for operational reasons the pilot has to make up his mind whether he will land at Gander or choose an alternative airport. The length of the runway definitely would be a factor in his mind. The fact that the jet age is not passing Gander by is very well illustrated by the fact that every week a number of jet aircraft land at Gander even with the handicap of what for these times is a comparatively short runway. I would ask the minister to ascertain how many of the larger jet aircraft use Gander at the present time.
Another good reason for the belief that Gander will continue to be used is the amount of freight that is handled there. Last Saturday, I believe, one of the large international airlines shipped 50,000 pounds of lobster and before the season is over they hope to ship a total of 800,000 pounds. That is one commodity alone which is being shipped from Gander. If my understanding is correct, air freight will play a very important part in commercial aviation in the future. As a matter of fact, it seems quite evident that the air transportation of passengers and freight is bound to grow enormously during the next few years. With this in mind it would seem to be a logical step to provide the great airport at Gander with one or, if possible, two runways adequate in length to handle the type of aircraft now coming into general use.
For a few minutes I should like to talk about communications on the Labrador coast. The coast of Labrador depends upon the Department of Transport for its radio communications system. The small settlements along the Labrador coast depend on radiotelephone sets for communication with the outside world. I have mentioned this matter on various occasions before. Communications on the Labrador coast are one of the matters which the Department of Transport inherited at the time of confederation. Truly the places are small and a comparatively small proportion of the population of Canada is involved, but nevertheless their problem is a real one. I would ask the minister to consider providing radiotelephones for Batteau, Williams Harbour,

Georges Cove, Fishing Ships Harbour, Spotted Island, Separation Point and Paradise.
These radiotelephone sets are small and comparatively inexpensive but their importance is very great. Their value is far out of proportion to their cost. As I have said, the communications system, through inheritance, is one of the services to be provided by the Department of Transport and I hope that in the near future these communities which are without radiotelephone sets will be provided with them. May I repeat that the cost is small but the value to the people concerned is exceedingly great. These sets may mean the difference between life and death, particularly during the long winter when the coast of Labrador is locked up tight.
With regard to airstrips, I should like to mention St. Anthony. The provincial government spent some money to develop a small airstrip at St. Anthony, one at North West River and one at Nain. Those at St. Anthony and North West River need money spent on them so that they can better handle planes particularly during the freeze-up and breakup periods. Again the amount of money required is not great but the need is most urgent. This is particularly so because these small airstrips will provide a means of communication with the hospitals on the Labrador coast and also will provide a means of transportation all year round for the people who live in these remote areas.
I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for St. John's East, in extending thanks to the minister for the icebreakers which have been serving a useful purpose in Newfoundland, especially in places in my riding like Botwood, Lewisporte and others. These places are deeply appreciative of the service of these icebreakers now located in Newfoundland.
Before I sit down, I should like to pay tribute to the officers and crews of the Canadian National coastal steamers which operate in Newfoundland waters. Naturally I am thinking of those that operate in my own district which extends from the central part of Newfoundland or which from a marine viewpoint, extend along the coast from Notre Dame bay to the northernmost part of Labrador. The crews of these ships are carrying on a very great service in the tradition of those seamen who for generations have served the coast of Newfoundland. In some parts of Newfoundland today other means of transportation are supplanting or supplementing the coastal steamer, but in northern areas the coastal steamer is extremely vital. These men are carrying on, as I said, in the great tradition of the crews of

such ships as the Glencoe, the Sagona, the Prospero and the Caribou, and they are doing so today in ships like the Nonia, the Springdale, the Burgeo and the Northern Ranger. These seamen are carrying out their work efficiently, with courtesy and kindliness and, above all, with a splendid sense of duty.
In conclusion I should like to go back to the question of Gander and ask if the minister could not find it possible to make a statement which will clarify what is likely to be the future of this important airport town.

I do not intend to take up very much time of the committee tonight, but I thought I should say a few words about air travel particularly because of its importance to Edmonton. Our new international airport at Edmonton is now at the stage where its runways, taxi strips and aprons are about finished and there appears to be a good possibility there will be air service out of that airport by the latter part of this year. I can assure the minister that we appreciate the thoughtfulness of his department in making sure that the original plans were changed in order that we might have runways built that would accommodate the largest and fastest long range planes that will be coming to Edmonton as a result of its position as the crossroads of the north. We have been playing a very important part in this field for years. I want to say that we appreciate the fact we will have a new airport which will assure we will be able to continue to play a very important part in long range air travel.
I am wondering a little bit tonight, however, about the local services. At the present time we have a very good T.C.A. service from Edmonton to Calgary. These two cities are less than 200 miles apart and, for years, Edmonton has had the good fortune of having a good city airport in the middle of the city. Its runways are not long enough to accommodate the modern fast transports, but they can accommodate the Viscount type of plane. The flight from Edmonton to Calgary takes about 45 minutes, and you are in the centre of the city within five minutes after getting off the plane. There are half a dozen such flights back and forth every day which accommodate a lot of people. We have a lot of businessmen out there with a lot of hustle who appreciate being able to do a day's work in another city and get back in the evening. Our new international airport is about 20 miles out of town and, depending on traffic conditions, this could mean a trip by taxi or limousine service of from half an hour to 45 minutes longer. A journey of this length by taxi is not much in relation to the long trips by air coast to coast or intercontinental 79951-0-282J
Supply-Transport
but in relation to a flight of 45 minutes duration the possibility of adding a 45-minute taxi trip is one that causes a little disquietude.
There has been no announcement by T.CA.. that they intend to discontinue the flights into the centre of Edmonton. On the other hand, they have not announced that they will continue to give service both to the new international airport and the one in the centre of the city. I think there are passengers for both, and I think both could be paying trips. I am hoping that T.C.A., when the time comes to move some of these facilities from the centre of Edmonton out to the international airport will not move them all. I hope we will still be able to have this quick trip to the very centre of the city of Edmonton.
There is a second aspect to this matter. I feel that the advantages in having an airport in the centre of the city are very great. I believe we are just starting that part of the air age in which vertical take-off flights and short run take-off flights will be coming to the fore. I feel it would be extremely hard to replace this airport. We hardly know or fully appreciate the value it may prove to be in the future. If there were to be a discontinuance of the operation of any major air line into our city centre airport this might weaken our arguments for the retention of that airport. There are other air lines such as C.P.A. and P.W.A. that are presently using this airport. I hope that T.C.A. does not set an example by moving its entire facilities out to the other airport.
I should like to say one more word about the new airport. The plans I have seen for the administration building at the new international airport indicate that it will be a credit, not only to the airport but to the country. Since Edmonton has been the northern centre for air transport for years, and since we have had many of the old bush pilots operating out of Edmonton who have done so much to open up the north and who have done so much for air travel in Canada throughout the years, it is hoped we could make a little gesture in memory of some of our air pioneers. There are plans for a plaque which they would like to have erected. I have brought to the attention of the minister a very suitable, large-sized wall space which I feel would be ideal for a mural. I hope that the small extra cost that might be entailed in making something really worth while and decorative out of that wall space will not deter the department from giving serious consideration to making this gesture to those who have done so much.

Mr. Chairman, in making a few, as usual, brief remarks on the minister's estimates, I must express my appreciation of

Supply-Transport
the minister's courtesy and the promptness with which he has dealt with any problems I have brought to his attention, regardless of the branch of his department which was concerned. One must give the minister credit for his industry. I also want to express my appreciation for the courtesy and promptness I have experienced in my dealings with the deputy minister. The deputy minister reminds me of the Baldwin apples I used to grow. He is a very firm sort of person. He is a long lasting type and he has an attractive colour. I have always been extremely pleased with my relationship with the deputy minister and with his staff and the head of the various branches.
We all realize that the minister's department is a large and rapidly growing one which is required to meet new problems almost daily because of the rapid development of our country and the changing circumstances from region to region or from area to area. The only suggestion I have to make with respect to the administration at this time is that possibly we are reaching the point where there should be one or two associate ministers in the Department of Transport, particularly in view of the great development of air travel.
However, I am not going to say much along those lines at the present time because the royal commission on transportation is conducting an investigation and organizations throughout Canada are making their representations. I have been extremely pleased to note that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made a representation on April 25 of this year and also British Columbia Tree Fruits Limited, representing the tree fruit growers of southeastern British Columbia, some time in February. I am sure we all look forward to this report. I think it would be more appropriate to deal with policy in general and with suggestions after the royal commission on transportation has had an opportunity to hear the representations made by various organizations across Canada.
However, before leaving my constituency to attend this session I was urged by a large number of the people I have the honour to represent to take advantage of the first opportunity I had to bring to the attention of the house a problem that concerns the people of southeastern British Columbia, namely the poor passenger service on the Kettle Valley railway. I have mentioned it on previous occasions. 1 want to take this opportunity again and keep my promise to the people I have the honour to represent.
For those who are not well acquainted with the geography of British Columbia I might say that the Kettle Valley railway is a railway that commences at Hope, a point a little
[Mr. Herridge.i
over 100 miles east of Vancouver on the main line of the C.P.R., traverses the southern part of British Columbia and ends at Medicine Hat in Alberta. What I am going to say this evening has the support of all the people of southeastern British Columbia, all the chambers of commerce, the associated chambers of commerce of southeastern British Columbia, all the trade unions in the area, all the farmers' organizations, all the municipalities affected and all the employees of the railroad concerned.
I have dealt with the details of this question previously and I am not going to repeat myself this evening. However, I wish to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the area which this railway serves is one of the richest parts of Canada as far as the production of natural resources from our forests, our mines, our lands and our waters is concerned. The total production last year in the area served by this railway was somewhere between $300 million and $325 million. Incidentally, I might mention that a great deal of that production was as a result of the operation of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited, which I note, according to the Nelson News of April 9, 1960 had profits in 1959 of $16,704,310. When you come to realize that the Canadian Pacific railway owns at least 50 per cent of the stock of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and as a result would make between $8 million and $9 million out of the company itself last year, without the profits of the railway which are considerable because of the freight transportation, the C.P.R. should normally have a great interest in the people in the area who produce that great wealth partly to the benefit of the Canadian Pacific railway. That is part of my argument.
I remember as a boy when sections were built to Kootenay Landing, then from Nelson to Midway, later from Midway to Hope and finally between Nelson and Creston along the south shore of Kootenay lake. The operation commenced in about the year 1911. It was a very well patronized passenger and freight service throughout the year. Of course, with the coming of good roads and other forms of travel there was a reduction in the number of passengers carried by the railroad until we finally found ourselves in the last year or two served by a Budd car. We have been reduced from a full-scale passenger service with sleeping cars, baggage cars, dining cars and all the rest of it to a Budd car with no sleeping accommodation, very frequently no coffee to drink and usually dry sandwiches. That is the position to which we are reduced in the southeastern portion

of British Columbia as a result of the refusal of the C.P.R. to recognize its responsibilities to the people of this area.
Naturally this state of affairs caused protests. The people of British Columbia have a habit of not lying down when they have something about which to protest. Anyone would have noticed that had he attended the recent convention of the Canadian Legion at Windsor, B.C. The delegates soon let their voices be heard as to what they thought about certain matters, as do the people of British Columbia generally. From what I can observe we are a little bit more active in voicing our protests than are some of the people say in eastern Canada. I am amazed at how quiescent some of the maritime people are about the problems in some areas which require immediate attention, problems which would create a real storm of protest in the area I represent. However, I represent a highly intelligent vocal people who expect certain standards maintained in transportation and services of that sort.
Protests have been voiced all over the district. Representations were made to the C.P.R. by the various organizations I have mentioned. I am quite sure the minister knows about the representations-he received a good many-to the board of transport commissioners; and naturally all of them sent copies to the member for Kootenay West because they depend on him to voice their opinions in this chamber and to put forward their views. In any event, as a result of the rumpus generally throughout the district- and as a result I think of the good offices of the Minister of Transport; I always give credit where it is due-the board of transport commissioners decided to hold a hearing.
The hearing was held at Nelson, B.C. on June 22, 23 and 24 of last year, at Vancouver on July 2 and at Ottawa on July 30 and December 8, 1959. The hearing was before Mr. H. H. Griffin, assistant chief commissioner; Mr. L. J. Knowles, commissioner-I do not want any misunderstanding; that is not Mr. Stanley Knowles-and Mr. J. M. Woodard, commissioner. The appearances included Mr. K. D. M. Spence, Q.C. for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; Mr. L. M. McBride, Q.C., for Nelson chamber of commerce, associated chambers of commerce, southeastern British Columbia, and joint running trades, railroad brotherhoods; Mr. A. L. Pearson and M. A. Weller for the attorney general of the province of British Columbia; Mr. Ken Smith, Mr. H. L. Robinson and Mr. Remo Morandini representing local 480, international union of mine, mill and smelter workers, Trail, B.C.; and Mr. T. S. Short-house, mayor of the city of Nelson, B.C. I
Supply-Transport
might say that all the business people I have spoken to, representatives of the chambers of commerce and so on, inform me how much they appreciated the well prepared brief by local 480 of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers. They had really spent a good deal of time on research and presented a well documented and logical brief.
The hearing was held by reason of dissatisfaction existing as to the train service being furnished by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on its line between Vancouver, British Columbia, and Medicine Hat via Nelson. The board gave notice that it would hold its hearing and receive submissions as to the service. The hearings were held on the dates I have mentioned. There was represented before the board in addition to the railway company the attorney general of British Columbia; the running trades, being the brotherhood of locomotive engineers, the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and the brotherhood of trainmen; the Nelson chamber of commerce; the associated chambers of commerce of southeastern British Columbia, which included the chambers of commerce of Kimberley, Cranbrook, Kaslo, Creston, Nakusp, Salmo, Trail, Rossland and also Lethbridge, Alberta; the Okanagan and boundary associated boards of trade, which includes as affiliated boards those of Summer-land, Naramata, Penticton, Osoyoos, Oliver, Keremeos, Rutland, Westbank, Okanagan Falls, Greenwood and Cawston; the international mine, mill and smelter workers, being Trail, local 480; Kimberley and Riondel, local 561; Beaverdell, local 900; Nelson and district, local 901; and Greenwood-Phoenix and district, local 1013. The members of these locals and their families make up a large part of the population of the Kootenays. Also represented was the Kootenay lake general hospital and the medical associated clinic of Nelson. A submission was also received from the association of Kootenay municipalities.
Mr, Chairman, I just want to deal briefly with the judgment. I want this on the record because I am sending a copy of Hansard to a number of people who wanted to get the details of the judgment and it saves a great deal of time in having all this copied.
Oh, oh.

I like to be frank about it, anyway. The summary is as follows:
Re: Service of Canadian Pacific Railway Company between Vancouver and Medicine Hat via Nelson, British Columbia.
The board of transport commissioners held a very complete hearing in this matter. The evidence was heard at Nelson, with subsequent adjourned

Supply-Transport
sessions at Vancouver and Ottawa. Members of the board travelled the line between Fort McLeod and Vancouver.
The board gave its judgment on January 4. 1960. It found that:
(1)	Since the service was begun in 1911, the railway company had made every reasonable endeavour to attract passenger traffic;
(2)	The present service (furnished by rail-diesel cars) is a curtailed one by reason of depredations and threats of depredations to the railway company's line;
(3)	A daily rail-diesel car service in each direction between Vancouver and Medicine Hat would meet the demands of the area, provided that reasonable amenities are furnished to passengers and provided that the travel time from Vancouver to Nelson would not be more than 15 hours;
(4)	The need of the residents of the area presently requires a daily service running (without any scheduled lay-overs) in each direction between Vancouver and Nelson.
The board would have ordered such service between Vancouver and Nelson if it had been satisfied that it would be safe for the railway company to comply with such an order.
Apparently it overlooked the fact that freight is going over the line daily and the employees are willing to operate the passenger trains. It continues:
It was not satisfied that it would be safe and made no order.
The province of British Columbia made a proposal toward the sharing of costs of further protection to be afforded to the railway. This did not result in any conclusion.
I do not quite know what that means. I continue:
The board concluded its judgment by saying that, at such time as
(a)	a sufficient time has elapsed without depredations occurring in the area as to remove, beyond reasonable doubt, the threat to the travelling public and to the railway, or
(b)	such protective measures have been taken as are, in the opinion of the police forces administering such measures, sufficient to protect the travelling public and the railway,
then, if the railway company has not, of its own accord, resumed a service which in the then existing circumstances meets the reasonable needs of the area, an application may be made to the board to require it to do so.
I understand, Mr. Chairman, that the city of Nelson is re-applying to the board for reconsideration of this judgment in view of the changed circumstances. I have been informed of that fact not only by the chamber of commerce of Nelson but by the secretaries of the various railroad organizations directly involved along the line of the Kettle Valley railroad and a number of other organizations and persons. Apparently the hitch in this thing at the present time is this protection to the railway from the depredations of some people.
I would also like to bring to the minister's attention this aspect of matter. In the Nelson News of March 3 I read the following;
Attorney general seeks Kootenay train service.
[Mr. Herridge.)
Attorney General Bonner intends to take up again with the chairman of the board of transport commissioners the question of renewal of fulltime train service through the Doukhobor areas of the Kootenays, he told the legislature Wednesday night.
The minister replied to Kootenay member questioners in the house that the province had offered to pay a third of the cost up to $50,000 of railway protection through the Doukhobor area, providing the federal government and the C.P.R. absorbed the other two thirds.
The board of transport commissioners had promised to make an order compelling the C.F.R. to restore full service "if we would guarantee the safety of the trains".
"But I want to say to the house that I can't really guarantee safety of your securities in your safes at night,... It is impossible to expect anyone to give an absolute guarantee under the circumstances.''
I think the Attorney General of British Columbia is correct in that statement. No one can give an absolute guarantee under any circumstances today with regard to almost any matter or question.
I rose tonight, after reviewing the case very briefly indeed, to suggest on behalf of my constituents and the organizations I have mentioned that we ought to have a satisfactory passenger service resumed on the Kettle Valley railway. The people in that area would consider it quite satisfactory if they had a Budd car, and a cafe-sleeping car, so that there would be provision for meals to be taken under civilized circumstances.
In this respect I might say that I had a letter only today from a member of the brotherhood of railroad trainmen, Kootenay lodge No. 558, Nelson, British Columbia, and I will quote part of this letter. He says:
According to today's paper the kettle is still boiling here by means of a resolution passed by the B.C. chamber of commerce at their 9th annual meeting in Vancouver supporting the much needed passenger service between Medicine Hat and Vancouver-
Then he adds a postscript:
Since writing this, it has been brought to my attention that a passenger leaving Calgary is unable to obtain as much as a cup of coffee until he reaches Cranbrook due to the transfer being changed from Lethbridge to Coalhurst. The service seems to be getting worse instead of better.
I have travelled on this train from Medicine Hat to Castlegar and from Castlegar to Vancouver. I have been on the train a couple of times when you could not even get a cup of coffee. On one occasion returning from Vancouver women with children could not get a drop of milk for their children, any sandwiches to eat or refreshments of any kind. That is not good enough on a passenger train travelling through the garden of Eden which produces some $300 million to $325 million worth of wealth in this country annually.

In conclusion I do urge the Minister of Transport to use his good offices and all his influence to secure a reconsideration of this matter, in view of the fact that the provincial government has offered to pay one third of the cost of police protection on this railway. This police protection is required because of certain incidents in the past on the part of a certain sect that reside in southeast British Columbia. I urge that the federal government matches the provincial government's offer and that the minister use his good offices with the C.P.R. In this particular instance that means Mr. Crump. I ask the minister to persuade Mr. Crump to take action, because I think we will get it. I knew of him as a small boy in Revelstoke many years ago but he has gone a distance above me now that he is president of the C.P.R. and I only a humble member of parliament. But I do hope the minister uses his good offices to get the cost of this police protection shared between the province, the federal government and the railway and obtain a resumption of a satisfactory train service on the Kettle Valley railway at the earliest possible date, in fairness to the people of southeastern British Columbia.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? How long has it been since one of his constituents bombed the railroad?

The hon. gentleman asked me a question which he knows is not true in the first instance. Even if he had asked me the question: how long is it since one of a certain sect bombed the railroad, I certainly would not be able to answer, correctly because it has not been proved to date exactly who caused this depredation, although there are certain suspicions. But I can assure the hon. member that the vast majority of the people of Kootenay West are very law-abiding and responsible citizens.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal with a problem peculiar to my riding, a matter which comes under the Department of Transport. For that reason, I shall not take too much of hon. members' time.
For more than a year, all operations on the Soulanges canal have stopped. Formerly, they brought a revenue of one third to one half million dollars a year to the citizens of my constituency, not counting the amounts spent by the crews of the ships using that waterway.
Supply-Transport
Since April 1, 1960, hardly $30,000 has been spent for the maintenance of that now disused canal. This is far from being adequate revenue for keeping the economy of the Soulanges area at the same level as in the neighbouring districts.
At this time, it would be difficult to justify the expenditure of a large sum of money for the maintenance of the Soulanges canal as when the waterway was in operation. On the other hand, it would be only fair to have some work done to renew the mobile equipment of the canal, like swing bridges and lock gates. It would be unfair if that waterway, which, when it was built divided the most fertile land of the Soulanges district and modified its economic character, were simply abandoned.
As the representative of that area, I have received numerous requests from municipalities along the canal. I think those requests are fair and reasonable.
Among the most significant requests in those submissions, I shall point out the following: That running water be maintained in the canal; that municipalities have the right to draw water free of charge therein to feed their water mains; that present bridges be replaced by jetties-I note that the estimates of the Department of Transport include an amount of $100,000 for the renewal of three of those bridges-that the lighting be maintained at the entrance of the jetties; that land adjacent to the canal never be used as a public or private dump; that passage for keeping up the flow of Delisle river, of Red river and Graisse river be maintained and regularly cleaned; that the fences of land adjacent to the canal be maintained and weeds be cut regularly; and, finally, that the land belonging to the canal be taxed on the same basis as property owned by individuals.
Moreover, three municipalities, whose boundaries run along the canal, approached me to ask that they be given priority when certain lots belonging to the canal system are put up for sale.
I want to point out to hon. members that since the Soulanges canal was closed to traffic no substantial revenue has come into the district. It is therefore justified that municipalities along the canal should ask some compensation from the federal government for the taxes they are not levying on canal property, which is estimated at some $230,000.
It is also reasonable to ask that swing bridges built for the type of traffic existing 50 years ago be replaced by solid roads built

Supply-Transport
for modern vehicles, and that the lock gates
in the two strategic spots, be replaced bypermanent structures. The cost can be justified by the fact that they would eliminate the maintenance required with the bridges and lock gates in their present condition, and the hazards involved.
Once those jobs are done, the towns of Dorion, Pincourt and ile Perrot could set up a corporation to instal the lines needed to supply water to their respective populations, which on the whole represent about 20,000 people. Such a project would cost about $1 million. Such a project could be worked out in two ways, either by setting up a company formed of the municipalities of Dorion, lie Perrot and Pincourt, or by a syndicate of private interests. At present, there are many of them who are prepared to form such a syndicate. .
From past experience, following the closing down of canals such as the former Welland and Beauharnois canals, I may state that it is in the interest of the government and the areas concerned to dispose as soon as possible of this disused waterway.
In addition to being used as a water system, the Soulanges canal properties could also help the development of housing projects and of suitable locations for the establishment of light and heavy industries. The eastern end of the canal, barely two miles from the St. Lawrence seaway, lends itself very well to the establishment of primary and secondary industries.
Upon completion of the bridges connecting Montreal island to the Vaudreuil peninsula, and incorporated in the future 401 superhighway system, there is bound to be extensive housing developments in that whole section of the Vaudreuil-Soulanges peninsula. The site will be a natural one for industries, provided municipal services are adequately planned. An adequate electric power supply added to the already existing manpower and perfect highways, only drinking water supplies need be added to make that section the most attractive in every respect in the entire Montreal suburban area.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to give very serious consideration to the dredging of a 25-foot shipping channel between the St. Lawrence seaway and the east or west limits of the Soulanges canal, in case industries should be located in that area and require the type of transportation which is common along the St. Lawrence seaway.

I have a few remarks I should like to make at this time concerning matters

which in my opinion are very important and urgent. Under this heading, Newfoundland again suffers. For example, the hotel accommodation at present available in St. John's, the capital of Newfoundland with an estimated population of over 80,000, is entirely inadequate. St. John's is the eastern terminal point of Trans-Canada Air Lines, the trans-Canada highway, Canadian National Railways and Canadian National Steamships. It is also the terminal point of the C.N.R. Newfoundland service. In addition, it is the point of entry into Canada for shipping coming from the British Isles and from Europe. All this shows the urgent need of a hotel with the necessary facilities to take care of the travelling public.
The Newfoundland hotel which is owned and operated by the C.N.R. is inadequate in its accommodations and facilities for the needs of the people of Newfoundland, quite apart from the claims of the travelling public, including representatives of the government and organizations in and near St. John's which require facilities for conventions, banquets, meetings, and so on. The result is that many conferences and conventions are steered away from St. John's. This state of affairs is bad not only for the economy of the province but also from the point of view of increased transportation revenue for the Canadian National Railways and from the point of view of public relations. Immediate steps should be taken to improve this situation by providing adequate accommodation.
It cannot be said that the Newfoundland hotel does not operate at a profit because it was only a few days ago that I asked the Minister of Transport if the hotel operated with a surplus or a deficit for the years 1958-59. The minister informed me that in those years the hotel operated with a surplus of more than $300,000.
In addition, the tourist trade which has increased considerably since confederation is suffering from this inconvenience. Coupled with this we still have our narrow gauge railway. We are the only province in Canada with a railway system different from that in the other provinces across the dominion. Newfoundland is, nevertheless one of the ten provinces of Canada. The present Prime Minister said that we should have a standard gauge railway and so I ask when is the government of Canada going to give Newfoundland her rightful place in confederation and put her railway and hotel facilities on a par with those of the other provinces. If this were done it would be a step in the right direction. I ask the minister if any serious consideration has been given to the statement made by the Prime Minister in St.

John's in April of 1959, a report of which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail in these words:
Newfoundland's narrow gauge railway should be converted to the standard gauge because the present line retards development, adds to the cost of transportation and therefore makes it more difficult for Newfoundland industries to compete in domestic mainland markets on the same basis as other provinces.
The people of Newfoundland have waited patiently for some action to be taken by the Canadian National Railways. In the light of this statement, surely after three years of study and consideration it is time to do something of a tangible nature to meet this great handicap. I would suggest that the minister have his officials make an investigation and estimate the cost of constructing a standard gauge railway from St. John's to Port aux Basques and then give the province of Newfoundland a grant for this amount which would have to be spent on the trans-Canada highway.
I am given to understand that there are two systems employed when planes make landings at airfields. One is known as I.L.S., that is instrument landing system, and the other is the G.C.A., or ground control approach system. The airport at St. John's should have all possible modern facilities. As far as I can ascertain the Department of Transport has one instrument landing system which I believe is used on runways Nos. 17 and 35. At the present time Trans-Canada Air Lines craft are more or less at the mercy of the United States officials at Pep-perrell air force base because they own and operate the ground control approach system by which planes can be talked to their landing places. Without this system the pilot must land his plane with the instrument landing system which does not allow him to land with less than a 300 foot ceiling and a forward visibility of one mile.
I appreciate the operational cost of the ground control approach but since the United States air force operates such a system and since they are vacating St. John's would it not be possible for us to buy this system which I believe is mobile. If this is not possible 1 would strongly urge the minister to install another instrument landing system at the airport at St. John's. I am told that the landing facilities there are the same today as they were 20 years ago and that no improvements have been made. With the ground control approach system planes could land with a 700 foot ceiling and one mile visibility. We have more hills and fog near the airport at St. John's than there are at many other terminals elsewhere in Canada. T.C.A. flights in Newfoundland are very popular and well patronized no doubt
Supply-Transport
because of the efficiency of the airline officials who are second to none throughout the dominion.
In my speech this year on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I made brief reference to the great need of a freight-passenger boat which would operate from St. John's to Halifax or Sydney. I cannot find words strong enough to point out the urgency and importance of the C.N.R. operating such a route. Many thousands living in Newfoundland at present hope and believe in the not too distant future we shall have most if not all of the trans-Canada highway paved. As soon as this highway meets trans-Canada specifications thousands of tourists will drive from the United States and mainland Canada to the east coast of Newfoundland. Would it not be reasonable to expect that they might wish to join a ship at St. John's and have a relaxing boat trip from St. John's to Halifax or Sydney rather than motor back approximately 600 miles from St. John's to Port aux Basques?
At this juncture I feel I must refer to the operation of the William Carson. When this boat began operating in Newfoundland a couple of years ago we thought she was too big and a waste of money. There was no doubt in the minds of many that she was more than able to look after all the passengers who cared to travel on her and was able to handle all auto traffic and commercial trucks and freight. Last year this ship carried approximately 8,050 passenger automobiles. There were 3,492 automobiles handled under the freight plan and 1,264 freight trucks. The ship made 288 round trips and carried many tons of freight. There were 37,841 passengers carried to and from Port aux Basques in 1958 and 58,435 passengers carried in 1959, an increase of 20,594. Last summer there were many times when the ship could not take care of all the passengers desiring accommodation for themselves and their cars.
Early last August my family had an experience which is a very common one to passengers and which 1 hope, should the occasion arise again, will be taken care of in a better way than it was last summer. My wife, two of my sons and myself arrived at Sydney on Sunday, August 2 at 10.30 p.m., half an hour before the scheduled sailing time. I immediately went to the ticket agent and asked if the reservations I had made in Halifax had been confirmed and I was told that they had no record of any reservations for me and that they would not be able to let me know until midnight whether we could get passage on the Carson. There was scarcely any standing room in the waiting room at North Sydney, much less seating

Supply-Transport
space. The room was crowded with passengers, many of them with babies and young children and many of them very much annoyed.
After making several trips to the ticket agent we were finally told that we could not get on the Carson but that the Burgeo was making a special trip from North Sydney to Port aux Basques to take the passengers desiring passage to Port aux Basques and that she would not be ready to sail until a couple of hours. Again the ticket agent said he could not give any assurance that we would be able to get on her. However, about 2.30 a.m. we were sold a ticket and we boarded the ship about 3.00 a.m. We found to our great dismay that no meals or lunches were being served on the boat and that there were but two stewards to take care of the passengers. We were fortunate in getting a room. Many did not.
About 8.30 a.m. we went to get breakfast but found that the salon was closed and learned that only approximately 50 per cent of the passengers, who totalled over 100, had breakfast. We arrived at Port aux Basques about 11.30 a.m. where a train was awaiting our arrival, and in a short time the train was in motion. We had to wait in line to get into the dining car and finally made it at 1.30 p.m. We then had our first meal since having lunch before leaving Halifax at noon on Sunday, the previous day. No meals were served on the train from Halifax to Truro or from Truro to North Sydney.
I tried to make a telephone call from the waiting room at Sydney to ascertain if I could get space on a T.C.A. flight but the telephones were out of order. I heard many of the passengers say that they would not make such a trip again or go through such an ordeal, and of course that goes for me as well.
Even at this time of the year if you want to go to Newfoundland or leave Newfoundland and travel by the Carson you cannot get accommodation when you require it. You must make your reservation well in advance. I would therefore ask the minister to see that proper facilities are available to take care of the travelling public going to and from the newest province of Canada so as to avoid disappointment to the travelling public and thereby avoid undue or unnecessary hardship.
I have learned recently that there are about 30 level crossing accidents involving trains and motor vehicles in Ontario alone each month, and I doubt very much that any thought is given to the strain and stress placed on a locomotive operator. This was very forcibly brought home to me last Sunday evening when, in travelling by train

from Toronto to Peterborough, I sat in a seat close to the operator and heard the whistle continually blowing. In my opinion motorists should exercise more care at railway crossings and should realize that a locomotive operator cannot swerve his train to avoid oncoming vehicles. He may apply his brakes, but as can be expected, he cannot bring his train to a sudden stop. I would therefore suggest that warning signals or stop signs be placed at all railway crossings and that the Department of Transport use every possible means to impress upon the public the importance of exercising care when approaching railway crossings.
At this time, Mr. Chairman, I want to thank sincerely the minister, his parliamentary secretary and his officials for their co-operation in sending icebreakers to the assistance of the sealing steamers whenever I made such a request. I can truthfully say that at all times I have received every courtesy from the minister and his staff whenever I have referred any problem to his department since becoming a member of parliament. I feel that he will appreciate some of these matters which I have brought to his attention this evening. I have one hope, that his department will improve conditions wherever and whenever he and his officials can as far as Newfoundland is concerned.
I also want to thank the minister and his officials for assisting the sealers travelling to and from their homes to join their respective sealing ships in order to take part in the seal fishery by giving them a reduced fare last spring, which was the usual practice prior to confederation and was known locally as the sealer's ticket.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have followed with much interest the statement of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) on his department's activities. I heartily congratulate him for the magnificent job he has been doing so far. I thank him also for the interest he has always shown in my constituency. I also thank the officials of his department for their remarkable co-operation.
My reason for speaking today is that 1 wish to deal once again with a project that is close to my heart and that I should like to see carried out, not for any personal or political advantage, but in the interest of my constituency and constituents.
Ever since 1957, when I was first elected to represent the constituency of Gaspe, I have been asking that a railroad be built between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts. I raised the matter in 1958 and 1959, and I raise it again in 1960.

I am confident that the Minister of Transport and the present government will grant to the constituency of Gaspe something it has never been able to get in the past and which is vital to its economic development.
That part of my constituency, which stretches over 320 miles, includes two provincial constituencies and part of a third. In the North Gaspe area, where the distance between Matane and Gaspe is 165 miles, there is not a single railroad.
Yet, my constituency is one of the richest in ore. It has a prosperous mine, the Gaspe Copper Mines, in Murdochville, and a number of others that would, no doubt, be put in operation tomorrow if we obtained the railway we want.
Mr. Chairman, I may add that, besides the Gaspe Copper Mines, various corporations that hold mining claims are only waiting for the railway to be built to put them in operation.
May I give a few instances: In Holland township, the Gaspe Copper owns 1,518 acres; the Miller Copper has 1,600 acres; the Gaspe Metals, 400 acres; the Horn Gaspe, 200 acres and the Holland Gaspe Mines, 920 acres.
In the Lemieux township, the Federal Metal Corporation holds 9,000 acres, the Peninsula Metals Corporation Limited, 2,000 acres; the Lemieux Mining Corporation, 800 acres.
In the Boisbuisson township, the Dubuisson Mines & Lake Opemiska Mines Limited owns 80 acres; the Standard Gold Mines Limited, 40 acres; the East McDonald Mines Limited,
4,000	acres; the Gaspe Exploration & Mining Company Limited, 800 acres.
Mr. Chairman, those are some companies that own large mining concessions in my constituency, which is clear evidence of our wealth.
One of the first mines to develop in Gaspe, the Gaspe Copper Mines, provides work at present for more than 1,200 employees.
Mr. Chairman, may I say that the development of other mines will materially help reduce unemployment, because it is in developing our country, and most particularly that area, as far as I am concerned, that we shall really achieve prosperity.
Mr. Chairman, the chambers of commerce of the Gaspe riding and a number of associations adding up to more than 10,000 persons have asked me to obtain the necessary fa-
Supply-Transport
cilities for the economic development of our region. Here is what those associations and namely the March 23, 1959 issue of the magazine Commerce have to say about this:
In relation to its population, Quebec is the economic area with the least railroad facilities or the most people per mile of railway. The number of people per mile of railway is 812 in Quebec, as compared with 519 Ontario, 418 in the mari-times, 359 in British Columbia, 148 in the prairie provinces and 369 for the whole of Canada.
And the article adds:
On the other hand, there are other opinions on the subject, such as those expressed by the province of Quebec chamber of commerce and those found in a bulletin issued by the Banque Canadienne Nationale.
They might be summarized as follows- there is no doubt that the province of Quebec is far from getting as favourable a treatment as other areas; with 30 per cent of the population, it has only 11 per cent of the railroads. Many of the lines running through it are just branch lines needed to link up with the Atlantic and the prairies. Why has the Abitibi not been linked up with Montreal by way of an extension of the Montreal-Mont-Laurier railroad? Why the delay in building the Matane-Gaspe line? Unlike Quebec, southern Ontario is covered with a network of lines serving industrial centres. Railway development has been particularly active in the western provinces. Ontario has twice as many tracks as Quebec, and Saskatchewan is close behind. It is obvious that eastern Canada, and particularly Quebec, has been neglected.
Mr. Chairman, I think that this article in Commerce is true. Therefore I still wonder, even now, why we waited so long to develop so wealthy a region which can help bring prosperity while we are now complaining about unemployment. I do say that it is by giving these mineral rich regions a chance to develop that we will help reduce and even eliminate the present unemployment, not only in our province but in the whole country.
Mr. Chairman, before I conclude my remarks, I would like to read an excerpt of a brief prepared by the Gaspe North chamber of commerce, of Ste. Anne des Monts, Gaspe North, about proposed construction of a railroad to serve Gaspesia. Here are the conclusions of this brief:
When we ask for the building of our railway, we do not have the Impression of asking a favour or a gratuity from the federal authorities; rather are we claiming our share of public services which the people of this area of the province of Quebec are entitled to expect from their governing bodies to ensure their economic expansion and the development of their natural resources at the same rate as in the rest of the country.
Let us recall the statement made in Toronto on March 17, 1949, by Mr. S. W. Fairweather, vice president of the Canadian National: "A railway must be considered in relation to the economy of a country, because a railway is essential to the prosperity of a State and promotes wealth. Those of us who live in large cities might be mistaken, but the miner, the woodsman, the fisherman and

Supply-Transport
the farmer are fully aware of the usefulness of a railway. New resources and new fields of activity are discovered every day that can be developed by railway facilities which are the life blood of a nation.
And the brief adds:
Mr. Geo. H. Hees, the Minister of Transport, himself recognized the need for the requested railway line between Matane and Ste Anne des Monts when he said recently in western Canada: "Railways are a prerequisite to and not a consequence of progress, as railways are indeed a factor of progress."
The Gaspe North chamber of commerce concurs in the views expressed by Messrs. Hees, Gordon and others on the occasion of the official opening of the Chibougamau railway, namely that: "Two factors are essential to our national economy:
1. The development of a number of our natural resources is still being held back by the lack of transportation facilities. 2. Our railroads can still be considered as pioneer installations, and are used to open up new areas of economic development".
Here is another statement by Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the C.N.R.: "In a country such as this, where distance is a vital factor in the cost of goods, you cannot think of developing natural resources without thinking of railroads."
Mr. Chairman, I am most surprised. I wonder if really Mr. Gordon was serious when he made that statement. If he really was, why did he refuse that to the Liberal party for so many years, even at the time when my hon. friend the member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) was Minister of Transport? Why did he refuse it, and why does he still refuse it?
Mr. Chairman, I can only hope that for once, Mr. Gordon will translate his words into deeds and will grant to the constituency of Gaspe what it has been demanding for so many years, namely a railroad.

I doubt, Mr. Chairman, whether there is any other department of government which impinges more often or more intimately upon the lives of the people of my province than does the Department of Transport. When it is realized that 99 per cent of my constituents live by the sea and that 90 per cent of them earn their livelihood either on the sea or from the sea it can be readily understood that they have a special interest in this department. I should therefore like to express to the minister on their behalf appreciation of the improvements which have been carried out in my riding during the last year.
I should like to express to the minister my personal thanks for the sympathetic way in which he has dealt with the problems which I have brought to him personally. I should

also like to express my appreciation of the co-operation which has always been forthcoming from the staff of his department both here in Ottawa and in the province.
When I went through my district in 1949 I remember compiling a long list of navigational aids which were required in my riding. Many of them had existed in years gone by but had been swept away by storms and other causes and had never been replaced. However, during the last 10 years a great deal has been done in this respect. The government -very wisely, in my opinion-insisted on rehabilitating the aids that were already in existence before supplying new ones. It was said that the provision of other aids could not be carried out properly until the department had been supplied with a boat which would be able to transport these aids and to service them. That boat has now been supplied and therefore that reason no longer exists. However, along the coastline in my riding there is still a gap where particular navigational aids in the form of light and whistle buoys are required. I hope that every effort will be made to supply as many as possible of these buoys in the coming year.
Many of the new houses which have been constructed as residential quarters for the keepers of lighthouses and fog alarms have been supplied with running water and electric lights but there still remain a great many lighthouses and residential quarters which do not have these facilities. I do not think these people should be compelled to wait until the building is reconstructed before these facilities are provided. These facilities are a normal part of our standard of living in Canada. A supply of electricity makes possible the use of many appliances which can lighten the work of the housewife and make life a little bit more bearable in these isolated areas. I wish the department would initiate immediately a policy of supplying every one of these residences with running water and with a Delco or similar lighting plants.
The hon. member for St. John's East brought to the attention of the minister the situation which exists on certain ships, particularly the icebreakers, with respect to the wages paid to the crews. These wages are based on the prevailing rates in the area where the men are recruited.
I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys last year, I think it was, when his estimates were before the house, and also before the Minister of Labour. This is a

situation which should be corrected but about which nothing has been done since this matter was last raised. It does not seem right to me that two people employed by the government on the same kind of ships doing exactly the same kind of work should receive a different rate of pay just because they happen to be recruited in different places.
This argument falls down completely with respect to captains and the masters of these vessels. I understand that there is a wide discrepancy in the pay of the officers on similar ships of comparable size just because they happen to be recruited in different places. This is something which ordinary justice demands should be rectified.
Another matter along this line which I should like to bring to the minister's attention is the situation with respect to assistant keepers. An assistant light keeper is not an employee of the department. He is employed, I understand, by the keeper and because he is employed by the keeper he has no status. He has no benefits of holidays or holidays with pay; I do not think he even qualifies for unemployment insurance. It is time that this situation too is corrected. I am informed that the minister's department is dealing with this matter on a sort of piecemeal basis by which about 50 of these people a year are transferred to the permanent list. That seems to me to be a very slow rate of progress. If we are going to go at the rate of 50 per year for all of Canada, then certainly it is going to be a very long time before this situation is corrected.
I should also like to express my support for the pleas put forward by the hon. member for St. John's East and by my colleague for Trinity-Conception for an extension of the Newfoundland hotel and for an alternative airstrip at Torbay. The hon. member for Trinity-Conception brought to the attention of the committee certain conditions which he experienced on the motor vessel William Carson which plies between North Sydney and Port aux Basques. I have always held the opinion that what should have been done in the first place was to supply two smaller ferries rather than one big one, but from my experience I know that the William Carson herself is not big enough to handle all the traffic available, all of the passengers who wish to travel at the peak period of the season. But what concerns me most is that the terminal facilities at Port aux Basques do not have sufficient accommodation for the travelling public.
In this connection I encountered last year a situation where a number of passengers were left in the terminal without any place to sit or lie down. Some of them were old
Supply-Transport
persons; three of them were patients who had just been discharged from the Corner Brook hospital. I personally spent hours trying to find a boarding house for them at Port aux Basques and Channel but without success because every place was filled up. So these people, old and young and some of them young children, had to spend the night lying on the floor in this new terminal, and that is a situation which should not exist in this day and age. Moreover it is a condition which can be very easily remedied because all that is necessary is for the Canadian National Railways to set up a couple of sleeping cars near the terminal and supply sleeping accommodation in that way. They can get meals at the terminal which also has sufficient washroom facilities, but as I say there is no place to lie down. I do hope the minister will bring this to the attention of the proper authorities and have something done about it.
The hon. member for Trinity-Conception mentioned the necessity of a standard gauge railway for Newfoundland. I brought this matter to the attention of Mr. Gordon when he was before the committee on government-owned railways and shipping and it was quite clear from his replies to my questions that he does not consider it his duty to take any initiative in this matter. According to him, the railway belongs to the government of Canada. He is merely acting as an agent of the government in managing that railway. He is prepared to carry out whatever rehabilitation of existing facilities is required to make the present railway adequate for its needs, but when it comes to a change of policy such as changing from a narrow gauge to a standard gauge, then it is very clear that he considers this decision ought to be made by the government and if the government makes it he is quite ready to carry it out.
As far as the point to point traffic inside the province is concerned, the narrow gauge railway perhaps serves very well. But when it comes to traffic entering the province and communications with the mainland, then the lack of a standard gauge railway imposes a very serious handicap on our economy. It adds materially to our cost of living and it handicaps our industries in shipping their products to the mainland market.
When it is considered that Newfoundland buys about $250 million worth of goods from mainland Canada it can be realized how essential it is to have those goods transported with the least possible handling and at the least possible cost. That can only be done by means of a wide gauge railway. Furthermore, Newfoundland is an underdeveloped

Supply-Transport
province and whatever possibilities it has for development will always be greatly handicapped unless modern means of transportation is supplied.
There is one thing about the Department of Transport which has puzzled me from time to time. That is this, there is a curious reluctance to make changes in the Canada Shipping Act or in other legislation or regulations which apply to this department. This, I think, is an attitude which is more characteristic of the Department of Transport than of any other government department. It seems to me that these laws are regarded as a sort of Procrustes' bed, or like the laws of the Medes and Persians which cannot be changed and ought not to be changed. Everything must fit into it. If you are a little too tall, you have to lop a bit off, and if you are a little short you have to be stretched out. Anyway, nothing can be done to change these laws.
One example of this is supplied by the laws which govern harbour administration. We have, of course, national harbours and we have certain laws under which they are administered. Then we have a class of small harbours that we call public harbours, and these are administered by harbour masters. Most of the harbours in Newfoundland are not big enough to be administered as national harbours and yet they cannot be administered satisfactorily by means of harbour masters under the public harbours act. For one thing, a harbour master is one man in an isolated spot far away from St. John's from which he would have to get advice in case something cropped up with which he could not deal. Sometimes, on a week end, St. John's has to get advice from Ottawa and when we close down early on Friday and wake up late on Monday a lot of things can happen which could not be dealt with at all. I have always felt the harbour master should be responsible to a local body on the spot in the community. We have such bodies. One such body is the pilotage commission. We have several pilotage commissions which are doing excellent work, and there is nothing wrong at all with giving them responsibility for harbour administration. It would mean a very simple change in the act to give them that power and it would not in any way interfere with their pilotage duties.
Prior to confederation we had small harbour boards of our own. These bodies do not know, at the moment, where they stand at all. They were set up under provincial legislation. At the time of confederation their sources of revenue were cut off, but they still have obligations which they have retained and which they have tried to discharge in the best manner possible. However, in carrying out these obligations they

have been at a very serious disadvantage. These small bodies could be recognized under our Canada Shipping Act and used to better advantage than is possible in the case of harbour masters under the public harbours act. I hope the minister will give some thought to this matter and assume a more flexible attitude toward these suggestions.
Another strange thing which I have never been able to understand is the regulation which prohibits a man from getting a master's certificate if he has to wear eye glasses. A person can get a driver's licence to drive a motor car at 60 or 80 miles an hour even though he may wear glasses. I think he can get a licence to pilot an aircraft at hundreds of miles an hour. But if he is going to get a licence or certificate to pilot a boat, to steer a boat or captain a boat he cannot get it if he wears glasses. But the strange thing is this: if he can once get a certificate he can go blind the next day and still retain it. The wearing of glasses simply prevents him getting a certificate. This seems to me to be a nonsensical state of affairs, and something should be done about it. Today good men are being prevented from getting a master's certificate simply because of this regulation, while other men, often less able, are qualified to get certificates.
Another suggestion which I made to the minister last year or the year before, I think, and about which nothing has been done, concerned the need for a change in the water carriers act in so far as it applies to C.N.R. coastal vessels. In Newfoundland we have a railway running in the interior, but most of my people live on the coast and the natural communications for them is by means of a coastal boat operated by the C.N.R. In other words these coastal boats perform the same service on the sea as do the railways on land. The same railway, the C.N.R., operates a boat from North Sydney to Port aux Basques. That boat is a part of the railway. The coastal boats which connect with this ferry, the William Carson, are not part of the railway. The William Carson, the ferry which runs across the strait, because it is part of the railway is not subject to the provisions of the water carriers act. The William Carson is not the only one concerned. There are, I think, as many as 10 or 12 ships on this run. Should any mishap occur to any of these boats, such as happened to the Cabot Strait some years ago when a lot of goods were lost because the ship ran ashore, since the ship was not subject to the water carriers act the people who lost their goods were given compensation. But should one of the coastal boats run ashore and freight be damaged or lost, the person who loses it has no redress at all,

because these ships are covered by the water carriers act. It does seem to be strange that the same company should be operating boats under two different arrangements when it affects the lives of the people in two different ways-that a person can have freight on one boat and if it gets lost he can get compensation, though if he has freight on another boat, owned by the same company, he can recover nothing should the freight be lost or damaged.
Before I sit down I want to remind the minister once again about the problem of oil pollution which has caused us a great deal of trouble in Newfoundland and which has become particularly acute during the past season. We all know that this is an international problem and that only an international solution will be satisfactory. There is, however, something which could be done. I do not know whether the minister has done it yet or not. However, I do hope he will be able to tell us when he replies that he has appointed a full time inspector whose job it would be to go around and inspect those vessels which transport oil and land oil on different points of our coast. There are some other points I should like to bring up but I have covered the main ones and shall reserve the others for another time.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if it would be in order for me to follow the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I have just been advised that he is leaving for the west coast this evening and wishes to speak. Would it be in order if he were to speak now and I were to follow him?

The hon. member for

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank my colleague the hon. member for Coast-Capilano for giving me the opportunity of saying a few words at this time. I have brought the problem of coastal transportation on the coast of British Columbia to the attention of the minister on numerous occasions and I wish once again to bring it to his attention. I do not know what the answer is but I do know there is a problem. To date I have not been able to convince the department that a problem exists. Once again I should like to request that a thorough investigation be made of this matter because it is serious and annoying and works a hardship on the residents of coastal communities.
We have a coastal transportation system now composed of antiquated and inadequate ships operated by a number of companies inadequately financed. Perhaps there is not sufficient traffic to support a private company operating on its own in those areas. In any event to a large extent the burden is passed
Supply-Transport
on to the people in the area in the form of high freight rates. For example, the cost of shipping a ton of potatoes to Port Hardy is often equal to the price paid to the wholesaler in Vancouver. The cost of freight on a loaf of bread is eight cents. The service is infrequently and completely inadequate. I suggest with all respect that at the first opportunity the minister appoint a team of investigators to come out west and travel the length of the coast, to interview the people served by these coastal services and listen to their story and to interview those providing the services and hear their story and then endeavour to come up with some solution to this problem.
When I look at the blue book-unfortunately most of our constituents cannot or do not look at it-one of the first things that impresses me is the millions of dollars that are spent in the maritimes, despite the fact that we hear hon. members complaining that more should be spent there; and the millions that are spent along the St. Lawrence as compared with the few paltry dollars that are being provided by the department for coastal transportation along the Pacific coast. I believe a subsidy is now paid amounting to approximately $300,000. I do not know whether subsidies are the answer but I am aware that the companies apparently are not making sufficient money to allow them to provide new and modern equipment and to furnish the necessary services at reasonable rates.
One of the unfortunate things about these poor, infrequent and high cost freight services on the coast is that they discourage people from living in that area. This would perhaps be all right if it were a non-productive area but it is a very productive area in the sense of producing raw material. I think I am safe in saying that the people who live on the upper coast of British Columbia are perhaps responsible for more dollar production of basic materials than any other group of people in any other section of Canada. I would ask once again that the minister give more than serious consideration to my request and that he appoint an investigating team to come out to the coast and make a thorough survey of the whole problem. I would even suggest that the minister come out and make a trip up the coast on one of our steamship services. I know that the hon. gentleman could pass over very quickly from Vancouver to Prince Rupert in a Viscount but he will not have any real understanding of the problems of the coastal area unless he travels from point to point on one of the obsolete steamships operating in the system we now have.

Business of the House

Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I inquire what the business is for tomorrow and as much of next week as the house leader may be disposed to give us.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
For tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, we will continue with the estimates of this department. Should they be finished in good time we have the estimates of the Post Office Department and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys available.
The legislative items for next week will be as follows. We will start Monday with the second reading of Bill No. C-58, an Act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code, order No. 5 on today's order paper. This will be followed by order No. 7 on today's order paper, the second reading of Bill No. C-63, to amend the Old
Age Security Act. The other items would then be No. 1 on today's order paper, No. 2 and No. 3 in that order dealing with harbour commissioners. The next item would be No. 17 on today's order paper, a motion standing in the name of the Minister of Agriculture referring certain business to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.
If that business is completed on Monday and Tuesday we would take up the budget resolutions on Wednesday and then on Thursday and Friday take up estimates starting with those of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and the other departments available. For instance, if transport were not finished we would take transport, post office, mines and technical surveys and fisheries. Any changes that have to be made in that tentative program will be announced in plenty of time for hon. members to adjust themselves to the change.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
